assignment.title: Fictional Exposure Consultation and Prevention Brief
assignment.instructions: Select one fictional scenario or public educational case link. Produce a 1,200–1,800-word consultation brief: exposure/source-pathway-timing map; developmentally appropriate differential and uncertainty; hazard-specific assessment/testing plan grounded in dated guidance; immediate and longer-term exposure reduction; referral/reporting partners; family-centered risk-communication script; evaluation measure. Do not include patient identifiers, real records or copied images.

rubric.excellent: Specific source, route, timing, settings and uncertainty are coherently linked.
Uses current primary sources, dates qualifiers, distinguishes hazard, exposure and causation.
Proportionate safe actions, needed consultation/referral/reporting and follow-up; no unsupervised treatment.
Clear, culturally responsive, feasible action plan and uncertainty statement.
Accurate citations; no copied protected material or real patient information.

assessment.format: Formative: 10 original questions, exposure-history worksheet, source appraisal and assignment. No pass-prediction or validated board-preparation claim.
assessment.rubric: Feedback based on source accuracy, exposure reasoning, uncertainty, referral and communication. Completion certificate, if independently offered, is not institutional credit, CME, board eligibility or certification.

studyHours.note: Study workload plan only (not recorded video hours): 12 units × about 6 hours (readings, notes, case practice and assessments) = 72h; introductory UNICEF/WHO course estimated 20–30h from its 10 thematic modules at 2–3h each, treated as interactive study time and not double-counted; capstone/assignment/review 18h. Individual time varies; this is a plan, not observed learner time.

topicGaps: No verified-runtime public, free-to-view specialist video hours can be counted from discovered candidate pages: playback/runtime verification failed on 2026-10-07 (YouTube HTTP 429/403).
No original videos are produced or counted. Recorded BCH Grand Rounds pages include password-protected Zoom recordings, which are not counted as free public video.

36h production gap remains at target. Interactive UNICEF/WHO course duration, slide decks, events listed as one-hour meetings, unknown video runtimes and proposed scripts are excluded from lecture hours.

Four new, relevant ANHE public recordings now have observed playlist runtimes (4:08:27 total); these are specialty-adjacent professional webinars, not a physician fellowship course, and their combined duration cannot stand in for clinical competencies.

The remaining 31.859 hours to the 36-hour video floor are not verified. Existing and new original clip plans are planned inputs only; their targetMinutes are not rendered media and are excluded from all hour totals.

Still insufficiently taught by verified recordings: advanced pediatric environmental exposure assessment and causal inference; current threshold-specific clinical pathways beyond introductory lead; private well/water and housing assessment; acute pesticide/toxicant triage; metals/solvents; climate emergencies and continuity; equity/policy; and environmental epidemiology/surveillance and capstone methods.

Several public candidate links (including the six original PEH-V recordings and EPA/CDC-hosted videos) lack a directly observed exact runtime or reliable unrestricted playback check; they remain in unknownDurationItems and contribute zero hours.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Non-ACGME clinical physician fellowship (packet classification; institutional directory marks No). Current Boston Children’s public page uses “Pediatric and Reproductive Environmental Health” and describes a combined BCH/Harvard Medical School two-year physician fellowship.
boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP): pediatric eligibility/certification is an institutional admissions prerequisite; no separate Pediatric Environmental Health certificate/exam listed.

American Board of Preventive Medicine (ABPM): Occupational and Environmental Medicine is a separately board-certified specialty with a separate eligibility pathway and blueprint; it is not this fellowship’s board exam.
American Board of Pediatrics co-sponsors Medical Toxicology certification with other ABMS boards; that separate certification is not conferred by this fellowship or course.
medical.boardStatus: No separate pediatric environmental health certifying examination appears in ABP current listed pediatric subspecialties. ACGME Pediatrics overview does not list pediatric environmental health as an accredited subspecialty. The named Boston Children’s/Harvard fellowship is clinical physician training; packet records it as Non-ACGME. Its required ABP pediatric eligibility/certification should not be misrepresented as a PEH board exam.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent self-study has no effect on ABP eligibility. BCH page states applicants must be in or have completed a pediatrics-related residency/fellowship and have ABP eligibility or certification in pediatrics. Confirm any current programme requirements directly with the institution. No separate board exam or guaranteed eligibility is claimed.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital / Harvard Medical School
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric and Reproductive Environmental Health Fellowship (official current page); packet’s exact item label is Pediatric Environmental Health Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page (accessed 2026-10-07) states two-year postgraduate physician programme; clinical instruction in pediatric and reproductive environmental health and environmental toxicology; didactics, clinical practice, community/public health engagement and research/scholarly activity; rotations at Children’s Hospital Primary Care Center and Pediatric Environmental Health Center. Tailored sites/interests. Page states PEHC sees >400 patients and 10–20 inpatient consults/admissions annually, but this programme page statement is not independently checked and no learner case-volume guarantee is inferred. The public page does not publish full course schedule or didactic contact hours.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet contains one official Boston Children’s offering. The current official programme page shows an actual clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory category or research-only job. The current official name is Pediatric and Reproductive Environmental Health Fellowship; preserve the packet’s exact item label Pediatric Environmental Health Fellowship. The fellowship page describes a combined Boston Children’s Hospital/Harvard Medical School programme. BCH GME directory categorizes Pediatric Environmental Health as Fellowship, Accredited?: No; ACGME’s Pediatrics overview does not list it among Pediatrics subspecialties. The fellowship’s public scope includes physician training, clinical service, teaching and scholarship. No separate pediatric environmental health board examination/certificate is listed by ABP. The ABP pediatric eligibility required for admission is not a PEH exam. Occupational and Environmental Medicine is a distinct ABPM board specialty; its certification pathway is separate and not awarded by this pediatric fellowship. No non-physician supplement is included.
sourceCaveats: No human clinical review performed. Clinical guidance is date-sensitive; CDC blood lead page checked as updated 2025-08-21; revisit live sources before use.
Institutional public curriculum is high-level, not a full syllabus. Stated rotations/activities are not a promise of access, patient volume, competency or credential.

Search results identified candidate lecture URLs, but public metadata/runtime and playback could not be verified due HTTP 429/403; every such item remains uncounted and is not represented as confirmed freely accessible.
BCH grand rounds page lists Zoom passcodes for many recordings. These are not treated as public free lecture links; no password content was accessed or counted.
AAP Green Book is copyrighted and commercial; no claim of free access. WHO slide sets have specific terms; do not redistribute without checking item license.

Case links point to educational resources; no actual patient data/images are copied. Authenticity, de-identification and reuse terms remain governed by source; do not download/re-host images absent permission.

BCH GME directory labels the pediatric environmental health listing Accredited?: No. This institutional directory label is reported as published, not treated as an ACGME-specific accreditation ruling; ACGME Pediatrics overview does not list PEH among its subspecialties.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which sample is needed to confirm a capillary BLL at or above CDC’s BLRV?

options.text: A repeat capillary sample only
A confirmatory venous sample
A hair mineral analysis
No further testing is recommended

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC directs clinicians to collect a venous sample when capillary BLL is at/above the 3.5 μg/dL reference value; follow threshold-specific confirmation timing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has a confirmed venous BLL of 8 μg/dL. Which plan best matches current CDC guidance?

options.text: Chelate immediately
Educate on exposure reduction, report per jurisdiction, take exposure history, assess iron/development and arrange follow-up
Discharge from follow-up because below 10
Obtain broad toxicology panel without source assessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: For confirmed 3.5–19 μg/dL, CDC recommends education, jurisdictional reporting, exposure history, investigation as required, iron status/nutrition, developmental surveillance and follow-up; chelation is not recommended at this level.

practiceQuestions.stem: A caregiver reports a child recently swallowed an unknown household product; child is symptomatic. Best first consultation?

options.text: Use online forums
Contact poison control/emergency services as indicated and obtain product/exposure details
Induce vomiting
Give activated charcoal at home

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute exposure needs expert triage based on exact agent, route, time and symptoms; do not advise emesis or home treatment. Use emergency services and Poison Control/PEHSU as appropriate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which concept best explains why the same environmental concentration may create greater dose per body mass for a young child?

options.text: Lower minute ventilation per kg
Higher air, water and food intake per kilogram plus age-specific behaviors
No hand-to-mouth behavior
Only inherited susceptibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: Children have higher intake per body mass and distinctive behaviors/developmental windows. These factors alter exposure and vulnerability; they do not prove that a particular disease is caused by a given exposure.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an environmental history, what is the most useful initial organizing approach?

options.text: Start with unstructured broad biomonitoring
Map source, pathway, route, timing, frequency and child receptor, then connect to symptoms and settings
Assume proximity equals disease
Ask only about current home address

practiceQuestions.rationale: A structured source-pathway-receptor timeline produces testable exposure hypotheses, prioritizes prevention and avoids over-attributing symptoms.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has asthma symptoms that worsen during regional wildfire smoke. What is the most defensible counseling?

options.text: Assert smoke is the sole cause
Discuss exposure reduction and asthma action plan, monitor symptoms, and account for local public-health guidance
Recommend all children wear respirators at all times
No action unless blood test confirms exposure

practiceQuestions.rationale: Counseling should be tailored to child risk and current public-health guidance. Avoid asserting sole causality from temporal association or giving blanket respiratory protection instructions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A family is concerned that a biomarker proves a specific illness was caused by an endocrine-active chemical. Best reply?

options.text: Biomarker proves source, dose and causation
Interpret biomarker validity, timing, reference range and clinical context; explain uncertainty and prevention options
Recommend commercial unvalidated testing
Dismiss concerns categorically

practiceQuestions.rationale: A biomarker can indicate exposure only within its measurement limits; it rarely alone establishes source, dose at a critical window, clinical effect or causation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A private-well family asks whether water is safe based on appearance and taste. Best next step?

options.text: Appearance establishes safety
Identify well and local contaminant risks and direct them to appropriate certified testing/public health resources
Rely on bottled-water marketing
Tell them no tests are useful

practiceQuestions.rationale: Many contaminants cannot be seen or tasted. Risk assessment and testing should be based on local hazards and competent public health/laboratory guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the appropriate interpretation of the Boston Children’s Pediatric and Reproductive Environmental Health fellowship for credentialing?

options.text: It is a distinct ABP board subspecialty
The current BCH/Harvard page describes a two-year physician fellowship; pediatric environmental health is not a separately listed ABP exam category
It confers ABP eligibility on any graduate
The training guarantees ACGME accreditation

practiceQuestions.rationale: Programme participation and board certification are separate. ABP lists exam-bearing subspecialties; its current list does not name pediatric environmental health. The programme itself currently requires existing ABP pediatric eligibility/certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which action best reflects ethical environmental health risk communication?

options.text: Promise that a proposed intervention removes all risk
Describe what is known, uncertain, actionable, and who can help, using understandable language and shared planning
Withhold uncertainty to avoid anxiety
Advise costly testing without explaining limits

practiceQuestions.rationale: Communicate evidence and uncertainty transparently, prioritize reasonable exposure reduction, and partner with family/public health without promising outcomes.

unitMap.text: Pediatric inflammatory bowel disease
coveredTopics: Initial workup; Porto-style diagnostic framework; phenotype; activity; nutrition; medications/safety; complications; transition
Revised Porto criteria: suspected PIBD evaluation integrates upper endoscopy, ileocolonoscopy and small-bowel imaging except typical UC after endoscopy/histology.

unitMap.text: Nutrition, growth faltering, enteral and parenteral support
coveredTopics: Anthropometry; malnutrition; feeding disorders; formula; enteral access; PN; intestinal failure; obesity
Nutritional decisions account for measurement quality, trajectory, family feasibility, and dietitian/team review rather than single-point weight inference.

unitMap.text: Pediatric hepatology and cholestasis
coveredTopics: Neonatal cholestasis; biliary atresia; metabolic/genetic; autoimmune; viral; MASLD; portal hypertension; acute liver failure
Infant jaundice after two weeks merits fractionated bilirubin; direct bilirubin elevation is a time-sensitive referral signal, not a diagnosis by itself.

unitMap.text: Biliary, pancreatic, and cystic fibrosis-associated disease
coveredTopics: Acute/recurrent/chronic pancreatitis; hereditary factors; gallstones; CF GI/liver/pancreas; enzymes and nutrition

unitMap.text: Intestinal failure, short bowel, and transplant concepts
coveredTopics: Short bowel; ostomy losses; PN complications; IFALD; intestinal rehabilitation; transplant referral; transition

unitMap.text: Diagnostic testing, imaging, endoscopy, and procedures
coveredTopics: EGD/colonoscopy; biopsy; capsule; manometry/pH-impedance; motility; ultrasound; MRI/CT; liver biopsy; ERCP
Match modality to a defined clinical question; describe why visualization or a normal test does not automatically settle etiology.

unitMap.text: Safety, ethics, communication, and health equity
coveredTopics: Adolescent confidentiality; feeding ethics; disability and culture; access; transition; safeguarding; quality/safety
Explain safety-netting and shared decisions without implying a self-study course can authorize clinical action.

unitMap.text: Evidence appraisal, research, and quality improvement
coveredTopics: Biostatistics; epidemiology; bias; consent/assent; research ethics; QI/PDSA; literature appraisal
Separate diagnostic-test performance, guideline recommendation strength, and expert opinion; date/source-check before application.

topicGaps: 36.00 of 36 target verified free recording hours remain unmet: no newly reviewed long-form candidate had both exact duration evidence and confirmed playable anonymous public video access. Do not count the surfaced metadata/transcript durations.

Coverage remains insufficiently expanded by openly playable recordings in foundational growth/development, diagnostic reasoning across stool/lab interpretation, constipation/cyclic vomiting, H. pylori, malabsorption, IBD biologic safety and monitoring, pancreas/cystic fibrosis, intestinal failure/PN, endoscopy quality, motility, research methods and universal tasks. Existing sources and original 48-clip plan remain available; source gaps are not converted into minutes.
The original 48 planned production blocks (2,160 target minutes) and new authored episodes are scripts/plans only, not rendered hours. No human clinician review has occurred.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Confirmed this is the actual pediatric clinical physician fellowship at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore, not merely the generic fellowship-directory category. The program page explicitly states ACGME accreditation and three-year duration. Its combined label refers to the division/service scope of pediatric GI, hepatology and nutrition, not a combined pediatric/adult board program. No second Harvard-affiliated offering or distinct combined residency/fellowship was included in the packet or independently verified in this one-item assignment. Research opportunities are part of clinical fellowship training, not a separate research-only/non-physician supplement. Pediatric transplant hepatology is a separate certificate and not folded into this specialty course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child undergoing evaluation for possible celiac disease has already started a strict gluten-free diet before testing. What is the most important interpretive issue?

options.text: Serology after gluten withdrawal may be less informative; clarify exposure and use an appropriate clinician-directed diagnostic pathway.
A negative antibody result after diet change definitively excludes celiac disease.
A positive HLA result alone confirms active celiac disease.
Immediate endoscopy is mandatory regardless of context.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reduced antigen exposure can impair serologic/histologic diagnostic sensitivity; use current guideline pathways and specialist judgment. HLA susceptibility is not itself a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age child has chronic abdominal pain, stable growth, reassuring examination and no alarm features. Which approach best reflects contemporary gut–brain interaction care?

options.text: Use a positive, biopsychosocial formulation with targeted evaluation and explain function; reassess if features evolve.
Order broad imaging/endoscopy before any clinical formulation.
Dismiss symptoms as fabricated because tests are reassuring.
Assume inflammatory bowel disease despite absent supporting data.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Functional disorders are genuine disorders of gut–brain interaction; a positive diagnosis, targeted assessment, validation, and follow-up avoid both overtesting and dismissal.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has progressive dysphagia and food impaction episodes with atopic history. Which next principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Consider eosinophilic esophagitis and use an evidence-based diagnostic evaluation including esophageal biopsies when indicated.
Diagnose GERD from atopy alone and never consider biopsy.
Treat as functional abdominal pain without evaluating dysphagia.
A peripheral eosinophil count alone establishes the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Symptoms and context can raise suspicion for EoE, but diagnosis requires appropriate esophageal assessment; peripheral eosinophilia is not diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a pediatric IBD diagnosis from isolated nonspecific inflammatory markers?

options.text: Integrate history, growth, laboratory/stool data and appropriate endoscopic, histologic and imaging evidence; markers alone do not establish phenotype.
A raised fecal inflammatory marker alone proves Crohn disease.
Normal growth excludes pediatric IBD.
A single normal inflammatory marker rules out all IBD.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Diagnosis and classification require synthesis; no isolated marker or normal growth trend has absolute rule-in/rule-out power.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an infant with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, what is the safest reasoning priority?

options.text: Treat cholestasis as abnormal and ensure timely evaluation for time-sensitive causes, including biliary atresia, while maintaining a differential.
Assume physiologic jaundice until school age.
Use a single ultrasound finding to exclude biliary atresia.
Delay evaluation until all symptoms appear.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia warrants prompt evaluation; a diagnostic pathway uses multiple clinical and testing inputs and urgency, not a single reassuring feature.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has recurrent epigastric pain and lipase elevation. What supports a careful pancreatitis assessment?

options.text: Apply accepted pediatric diagnostic criteria and integrate characteristic pain, enzymes and imaging rather than overinterpreting any one element.
Label all recurrent abdominal pain pancreatitis.
Diagnose chronic pancreatitis from one mild enzyme elevation.
Ignore alternative etiologies if pain is present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pancreatitis diagnosis requires a defined combination of findings; a single symptom or minor enzyme abnormality is not sufficient. Use current specialty guidance and clinical judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow learner watches an endoscopy video and completes a quiz. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: The learner has demonstrated knowledge in the exercise, not independent procedural competence or credentialing.
Video observation establishes endoscopic competency.
Passing a self-study quiz authorizes clinical procedures.
Competency can be inferred from course completion alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Procedural skill requires supervised training and formal assessment; this independent curriculum does not confer privileges, case volume or competence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 17-year-old with IBD shares sensitive information in a visit. What should the educational case analysis emphasize?

options.text: Apply jurisdictional/institutional confidentiality, consent/assent, safety exceptions and developmentally appropriate shared decision-making.
Promise absolute secrecy regardless of safety risks or law.
Exclude the adolescent and speak only to caregivers.
Assume adult confidentiality law applies identically in every setting.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adolescent privacy requires context-sensitive application of law and policy, explanation of confidentiality limits, and respectful engagement.

practiceQuestions.stem: A study reports association between a diet and improved symptoms in an uncontrolled cohort. What is the strongest inference?

options.text: The association is hypothesis-generating; confounding, selection and regression to the mean limit causal claims.
The diet caused improvement in all patients.
No useful information can be learned from observational data.
Statistical significance eliminates bias.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Study design determines causal strength; observed association is not proof of causality and must be appraised for bias and applicability.

practiceQuestions.stem: A candidate asks if this course plus independent study meets ABP Pediatric GI certification eligibility. Which answer is correct?

options.text: No. ABP requires qualifying accredited fellowship training, verification/scholarly activity and passing its subspecialty exam; independent study cannot confer eligibility.
Yes, if 36 video hours are completed.
Yes, because the program page states a three-year fellowship.
Eligibility is determined by the course provider.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP criteria require three years full-time broad-based accredited training, program verification and scholarly activity, and passing the ABP Pediatric Gastroenterology examination. This self-study course is unaffiliated and not accredited training.

topicGaps: Verified external footage remains 11.1558 hours, leaving 24.8442 hours to the 36-hour target; no authored target minutes are counted as video.

Four newly authored source-grounded scripts (one introductory and three worked-reasoning episodes) improve coverage in ALL evidence reasoning, T-ALL/T-LBL differential, HSCT/cellular-therapy evidence interpretation, and survivorship; they remain scripted and not rendered.

Lecture ledger is uneven: 8 added St. Jude talks are concentrated in leukemia, cell/gene therapy, brain tumors, access and survivorship; they do not supply verified didactic depth across erythrocyte disorders, HLH, marrow failure, transfusion, hemophilia/VWD/thrombosis, AML management, the full lymphoma/sarcoma/renal/liver tumor spectrum, emergencies, ethics/QI and scholarly methods.

Public programmes do not disclose complete block-by-block didactics. The Johns Hopkins/NCI joint course description remains a programme overview, not an auditable lecture inventory; the ABP outline is an exam blueprint, not a curriculum.

Board-topic detail and clinical recommendations can change. A human pediatric hematology-oncology clinician has not reviewed these additions; current protocols, trial evidence, product labels and local practice require qualified review.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — Pediatric Hematology-Oncology subspecialty examination
medical.boardStatus: Distinct pediatric subspecialty certification exam administered by ABP; separate from general pediatrics certification. Training and eligibility requirements are determined by ABP.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course confers no board eligibility. ABP requires three years of qualifying fellowship, scholarly activity, training verification and a passing separate subspecialty exam, in addition to its general and subspecialty-specific criteria. Check current board rules. ACGME entry criteria and limited exceptions do not themselves guarantee board eligibility. Institutional dual-board options require separate confirmation with both boards.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine / National Cancer Institute, NIH
officialProgrammes.name: Johns Hopkins University/National Institutes of Health Pediatric Hematology-Oncology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official joint clinician-researcher fellowship. Hopkins describes year one as 11 months clinical and one vacation month, monthly blocks without a named list in retrieved text, protected research in years 2–3 with continuity clinic/weekends, and optional fourth-year research or focused non-malignant heme, neuro-oncology, sarcoma, BMT or cellular therapy. NCI confirms year-one clinical training at both Hopkins Hospital and NIH Clinical Center and later research opportunities. Not a complete published block curriculum or ACGME audit.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One joint institutional programme variant (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and NCI/NIH). It is not counted as separate Hopkins and NCI fellowships. No Harvard offering appeared in this supplied specialty packet. No research-only, non-physician or generic supplement included. Hopkins mentions optional adult/pediatric and pediatric/palliative dual-board training; detailed requirements not established.
sourceCaveats: No prior MED-159 programme files or saved research files were present at the named paths; no previous verified research could be reused.

The supplied packet contains one Johns Hopkins University/NCI/NIH joint clinical physician fellowship. It is one joint programme variant, not two independent offerings. No Harvard-affiliated programme variant was in this packet; this file does not claim a full cross-institution directory.

This is a real physician specialty fellowship, not generic category, research-only job or non-physician supplement. Hopkins and NCI describe the joint clinical programme. Dual-board options are mentioned institutionally, but their precise criteria were not established here.

ABP provides a distinct Pediatric Hematology-Oncology subspecialty certifying examination. The ABP page requires qualifying fellowship, scholarly activity, training verification and passing the examination. General and subspecialty criteria both apply. ACGME permits pediatrics or combined internal medicine-pediatrics residency as programme prerequisite; its narrow exceptional IMG provision does not ensure ABP certification eligibility.

ACGME requirements effective 2026-07-01 say 36 months and at least 12 months dedicated research/scholarly activity. Hopkins public curriculum describes first year and protected years 2–3 but not named monthly blocks in the retrieved text. No case volume, rotation quota or institutional compliance claim is made.

ABP outline for current exams remains effective to March 30, 2027. New outline applies starting March 31, 2027, explicitly includes cellular/gene therapy in domain 10 and shifts some weights. Current exam mapping depends on exam date.

Only three unique free public lecture recordings with directly observed runtimes count. Rutgers Session 2 was listed in the public playlist but the direct public watch page said unavailable. Six Children’s Colorado embedded lectures had page-level topic labels but no observed runtime, so not counted. Titles for Rutgers sessions 1 and 3 disclose no detailed disease content; these are broad field hours only.

ASH case pages are authentic source-hosted resources. Public viewing is not reuse permission. Patient age and de-identification details were not independently verified; no images or patient records are copied.

Clinical recommendations/regulatory status change. Check current NCI PDQ, ASH, NHLBI, FDA and local protocols before clinical use. No dose, order or individualized treatment recommendation is provided.

Human clinical review has not been performed. Independent self-study gives no affiliation, accredited training or credit, licensure, board eligibility, clinical/procedural competence or certification; it cannot guarantee passing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child has anemia and microcytosis on one CBC. What is established?

options.text: Iron deficiency is confirmed.
Red cells are small; this narrows but does not settle etiology.
Thalassemia is confirmed.
Hemolysis is excluded.

practiceQuestions.rationale: MCV describes red-cell size, not etiology; iron disorders, thalassemia and other causes remain.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional anemia has inadequate reticulocyte response for its degree. Best interpretation?

options.text: Proves immune hemolysis.
Supports an insufficient regenerative response at that time and prompts production-side differential.
Proves recent bleeding.
Excludes marrow disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reticulocyte response organizes regenerative versus hypoproliferative patterns but is not independently diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has bleeding, prolonged aPTT and normal PT. Best next reasoning?

options.text: Diagnose hemophilia without work-up.
Use phenotype and confirmatory studies to distinguish factor deficiency, inhibitor or other cause.
Conclude thrombocytopenia.
Assume DIC.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening assays inform a differential but do not independently identify a specific cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is an appropriate isolated thrombocytopenia differential?

options.text: Only immune thrombocytopenia.
Artifact, destruction, production, sequestration and inherited causes.
Platelet function cannot matter.
Count alone defines function.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint distinguishes thrombocytopenia considerations and acquired/inherited number and function disorders.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement distinguishes autologous from allogeneic HSCT?

options.text: Autologous donor graft; allogeneic self cells.
Allogeneic donor cells can add graft-versus-tumor effect; autologous returns the patient’s own stored cells after high-dose treatment.
Neither requires relapse-risk review.
All cancers require HSCT.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ describes these distinct mechanisms and disease-specific indication comparisons.

practiceQuestions.stem: What bias may affect an observational HSCT versus chemotherapy outcome comparison?

options.text: Time-to-transplant and selection bias, including remission and ability to reach transplant.
No cohort bias possible.
Randomization by definition.
Only assay error.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ highlights remission status, time-to-transplant and selection bias.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is an ABP content outline?

options.text: Guaranteed complete clinical curriculum.
Exam blueprint, not official curriculum or guarantee of readiness.
ACGME accreditation document.
Board eligibility award.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP cautions its outlines are not study guides or curriculum guides; eligibility is separate.

practiceQuestions.stem: For current SCD qualifiers, what source strategy is safest?

options.text: Use a dated social post alone.
Check current ASH/NHLBI guidance and current regulatory status; do not assume old therapies remain available.
Assume every historical medicine remains approved.
Use this course as protocol.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guidelines and regulatory status change; NHLBI notes voxelotor withdrawal in 2024.

practiceQuestions.stem: May an open independent course download an ASH Image Bank picture because the page is public?

options.text: Yes, viewable means open license.
No; link to the source and obtain permission for reuse because ASH retains copyright.
Remove watermark.
Assume Creative Commons.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ASH terms limit copying and rehosting; accredited classroom permission does not grant this independent online course reuse.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which distinction between accreditation and certification is correct?

options.text: ACGME accredits training programmes; ABP separately determines individual certification under its eligibility and exam rules.
A programme web page certifies.
A 36-hour course grants eligibility.
ABP accreditation replaces ACGME.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Accreditation and individual board certification are separate systems and this course awards neither.

assignment.title: Inpatient clinical reasoning, safety and improvement portfolio
assignment.instructions: For one constructed fictional inpatient vignette, submit a one-page prioritized differential/risk representation, evidence-linked evaluation and monitoring rationale, family communication/discharge handoff, escalation and supervision plan, and a 1-page QI proposal with aim, operational definition, process/outcome/balancing measures and equity check. Alternative: analyze the linked public AHRQ hospital QI case study without adding patient-level material.

rubric.clinical_reasoning_and_safety: 40% — prioritization, uncertainty, red flags and escalation; no unsupported certainty.
rubric.evidence_and_applicability: 25% — current source quality, population/context limits, explicit update check.
rubric.family_coordination_and_transition: 20% — interpretable shared plan, follow-up and closed-loop handoff.
rubric.QI_design: 15% — measurable aim, sound measure definitions, systems framing and equity consideration.

assignment.rights: Fictional vignettes only; never include real patient information, identifiable images or copied proprietary cases.

assessment.format: 12-unit formative case write-ups, 10 original multiple-choice questions, one integrative portfolio assignment and reflective gap log.
assessment.passing: No validated exam cutoff or predictive claim. Local course completion threshold may be chosen only for course administration and cannot imply board competence.
assessment.assessmentRubric: Assess reasoning, evidence, safety, communication and limitations; give corrective feedback with current references. Neither MCQs nor self-assessment replace clinical evaluation.

unitMap.text: Clinical reasoning, acuity and inpatient work
coveredTopics: Synthesize developmental context, problem representation, illness scripts, prioritized differentials, risk assessment and reassessment. Distinguish escalation triggers from diagnostic certainty.

unitMap.text: Respiratory and infectious presentations
coveredTopics: Compare bronchiolitis, asthma, pneumonia, upper-airway obstruction and respiratory failure; choose proportionate testing/support, evaluate sepsis/infection and steward antimicrobials.

unitMap.text: Cardiovascular, shock and neurologic emergencies
coveredTopics: Recognize compensated shock, altered mental status, seizure, meningitis/encephalitis, heart failure and arrhythmia; stabilize, investigate and coordinate escalation without overclaiming certainty.

unitMap.text: GI, renal, endocrine, hematology and acute surgical co-management
coveredTopics: Build safe differentials for dehydration/electrolyte disturbance, AKI, abdominal emergencies, diabetes/metabolic illness, bleeding, thrombosis and sickle-cell complications; request surgical/subspecialty input.

unitMap.text: Newborn care and early infancy
coveredTopics: Apply age-specific physiology to newborn transition, jaundice, feeding, hypoglycemia, fever and common neonatal conditions; identify time-sensitive evaluation and nursery-to-home follow-up needs.

unitMap.text: Behavioral health, development and child maltreatment

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 7-week-old has fever at home, is now afebrile in the emergency department, and appears well. Which principle should guide the inpatient learner’s next step?

options.text: A normal appearance excludes invasive bacterial infection.
Apply a current age-stratified febrile-infant pathway and assess age, appearance, history and testing criteria; do not use one finding as a rule-out.
Diagnose viral illness if a sibling has a cold.
Delay evaluation until fever recurs.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Age-specific risk and protocol thresholds matter; an afebrile snapshot or exposure does not independently exclude serious infection. Confirm the current institutional/AAP pathway because recommendations evolve.
practiceQuestions.domain: Medical conditions—fever in young infant; diagnosis/risk assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 5-month-old with typical bronchiolitis has mild-moderate work of breathing, stable oxygenation and adequate hydration. Which is the highest-value approach?

options.text: Routine chest radiograph, viral panel and antibiotics.
Supportive assessment/monitoring and hydration/airway support tailored to severity; avoid routine tests/antibiotics when uncomplicated.
Scheduled bronchodilator for every infant.
Chest physiotherapy to prevent pneumonia.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The inpatient UCSF consensus guideline and CDC summary support avoiding routine testing and ineffective therapies in uncomplicated bronchiolitis; current local oxygen/feeding escalation criteria must be checked.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age child admitted with pneumonia is worsening despite initial treatment. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Continue identical treatment because radiographic pneumonia always resolves slowly.
Reassess physiology, diagnosis, complications, adequacy/adherence of therapy and need for escalation/consultation.
Broaden antibiotics without reassessment.
Obtain daily imaging until discharge.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical deterioration requires reassessment of the differential and trajectory, not automatic continuation or indiscriminate broadening/testing. Use current local and national guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with vomiting and tachycardia has delayed capillary refill. What should the team prioritize?

options.text: A single laboratory value to classify shock definitively.
Immediate structured assessment of perfusion/airway/breathing, serial response, likely causes and timely escalation while seeking help.
Fluid bolus at an unreviewed fixed volume for all children.
Wait for hypotension before escalation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric shock may be compensated; management is age-, cause- and response-dependent and requires current resuscitation protocol and senior support. This question deliberately does not prescribe a dose.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn is visibly jaundiced before discharge. Which is the safest educational action?

options.text: Use visual assessment alone to determine bilirubin risk.
Use age-in-hours, gestational age and measured bilirubin with the current neonatal hyperbilirubinemia guideline and follow-up plan.
Discharge without follow-up if feeding once.
Treat every visible jaundice identically.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hyperbilirubinemia decisions are time- and risk-specific. Consult current AAP neonatal guidance and local pathway; visual color alone cannot determine treatment threshold.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with a complex chronic condition is admitted. Which first step best supports family-centered planning?

options.text: Assume prior plans are current and family priorities do not matter.
Reconcile baseline function, family goals, communication/access needs, home technology/support and contingency plans with the child/family and team.
Defer all decisions to one consultant.
Use a standard discharge checklist without individualized input.

practiceQuestions.rationale: PHM practice includes collaborative, family-centered care and coordination for medical complexity. The plan should integrate family-defined priorities and appropriate team input.
practiceQuestions.domain: Children with medical complexity; patient/family-centered care.

practiceQuestions.stem: During handoff, a patient may deteriorate overnight. Which handoff feature best reduces avoidable ambiguity?

options.text: A long unprioritized problem list.
Concise illness summary, current status, contingency triggers, explicit actions/ownership and closed-loop opportunity for questions.
Only verbal mention with no receiver confirmation.
Tell the receiving clinician to reread the whole chart.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME milestones emphasize standard templates, effective transitions and closed-loop communication in complex settings.

practiceQuestions.stem: A medication error reached a patient but caused no apparent harm. What is the best systems-oriented response?

options.text: Blame the last person who touched the medication.
Ensure immediate patient assessment and appropriate disclosure/reporting through local policy, then examine contributing system factors and learn.
Omit reporting because no harm is obvious.
Alter the record to avoid alarm.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Patient safety response prioritizes patient welfare, truthful documentation/disclosure consistent with law/policy, reporting and system learning, not blame or concealment.

practiceQuestions.stem: An asymptomatic child with uncomplicated bronchiolitis is being considered for antibiotics. Which evidence-based stewardship response is best?

options.text: Antibiotics prevent bacterial superinfection in all infants.
Reassess for a separate bacterial indication; antibiotics are not helpful for bronchiolitis itself.
Prescribe because viral testing is positive.
Use broader therapy to shorten symptoms.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC’s pediatric outpatient summary says antibiotics do not help bronchiolitis; inpatient clinical decisions still require evaluation for a distinct bacterial process and applicable local guidance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trainee sees an unusual imaging finding on an online case website. What is a lawful course for a course assignment?

options.text: Download many images and rehost them because viewing is free.
Link to one case and discuss it; if reproducing an image, verify the specific license, noncommercial/share-alike terms and attribution, and do not scrape or republish outside the license.
Remove the watermark and cite the website only.
Upload a real patient scan to a public case site without checking consent.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia Terms impose content-specific modified CC license terms and prohibit scraping; no real patient images or protected records should be rehosted without lawful authority.

prerequisites.intendedLevel: Postgraduate physician-level self-study for pediatric residents, pediatric infectious disease fellows, and clinicians reviewing the ABP PID blueprint; not an entry-to-medicine curriculum.
assumedKnowledge: Medical school foundations in microbiology, immunology, pharmacology, pediatrics and clinical epidemiology.
Clinical reasoning and basic interpretation of cultures, molecular assays, susceptibility results and vaccine schedules.
Supervised physician training for any application to individual care.
prerequisites.sequence: Read the ABP outline and source/date caveats first; proceed Units 1–12; use each current guideline as the clinical authority; attempt original questions after each unit; revisit units using source updates.

objectives: Map learning across all 22 ABP pediatric infectious diseases domains using the official 2025-effective outline.
Build age-, host-, exposure- and timeline-aware infectious differentials and state evidence limitations.
Interpret microbiology, resistance, clinical research, stewardship, prevention and current guidelines with diagnostic restraint.
Practice safe, source-cited communication and appraisal rather than individual patient care or prescribing.
Distinguish public institutional training descriptions, ACGME training standards and ABP board blueprint/eligibility.

units.title: Clinical ID consultation, host-pathogen reasoning and test interpretation
objectives: Construct a pediatric ID problem representation integrating age, immune status, time course, anatomy, exposures and prior antimicrobials.
Select a discriminating differential and explain how specimen quality, prior therapy and pretest probability affect interpretation.
Distinguish infection from colonization, contamination and inflammatory mimics.
topics: Consult question and clinical reasoning; sensitivity/specificity, specimen collection, stains, culture, antigen, molecular testing, serology, susceptibility and resistance phenotype/genotype.
units.casePractice: Fictional: compare competing hypotheses for a child with prolonged fever and an equivocal multiplex assay. State what additional history/specimen changes the probability.
units.assessment: One-page consult note: representation, ranked differential, test utility/limitations and stop/reassess trigger. Rubric: reasoning 40%, test interpretation 30%, uncertainty/safety 20%, clarity 10%.

units.title: Antimicrobial principles and pediatric stewardship
objectives: Relate mechanism/resistance class, age-specific pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics, adverse effects and allergies to an antimicrobial decision framework.
Explain empiric versus targeted therapy, de-escalation, source control, route and duration review, and diagnostic stewardship.
Interpret stewardship literature without turning a small cohort into an individual treatment recommendation.
topics: Antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic principles; allergy labels; therapeutic monitoring; narrow-spectrum choices; audit/feedback; source control.
units.casePractice: Fictional: review a complicated-child pneumonia vignette with an antibiotic order timeline; identify where data permit narrowing and where the case facts are insufficient.
units.assessment: Stewardship memo plus a 5-slide M&M: validity of diagnosis, drug spectrum/host factors, de-escalation, source control, follow-up and measured balancing outcomes. Rubric: evidence 35%, stewardship analysis 30%, safety 25%, communication 10%.

units.title: Infections in immunocompromised hosts and device/transplant settings
objectives: Differentiate risks across primary immune defects, malignancy/neutropenia, biologics, stem-cell/solid-organ transplant, HIV and anatomic host factors.
Generate an exposure- and timeline-aware differential for fever in a high-risk host.
Describe the role of diagnostic microbiology, prophylaxis, infection prevention and multidisciplinary consultation without prescribing a regimen from memory.
topics: Primary and acquired immunodeficiency, central line/device and post-surgical infection, donor-derived risk, transplant-associated infection, malignancy and febrile neutropenia, cystic fibrosis.
units.casePractice: Fictional: child after hematopoietic cell transplant with new fever and pulmonary findings. Prioritize key host/time/exposure facts and immediate team communication questions.
units.assessment: Host-risk matrix with one-page case defense; explicitly label treatment decisions that require local protocol/consultation. Rubric: host-risk linkage 35%, differential 25%, test plan 20%, limits/escalation 20%.

units.title: Fetus, neonate and febrile young infant
objectives: Organize congenital, intrapartum, early/late postnatal and young infant infection risks by chronology and exposure.
Compare the logic of age-stratified febrile-infant pathways without substituting an old video for current protocols.
Identify where maternal, perinatal and neonatal history changes the diagnostic frame.
topics: Congenital CMV, syphilis, HIV and other congenital infection; neonatal HSV, perinatal exposure, sepsis/meningitis; febrile infant evidence and pathophysiology.
boardDomains: Prevention and containment of infectious diseases (8%)
units.casePractice: Fictional: well-appearing young infant with fever and a maternal/perinatal exposure detail. Learner identifies which facts are time-sensitive and why current age-specific local algorithms govern.
units.assessment: Timeline-based differential and evidence summary; no treatment orders. Rubric: chronology 30%, risk stratification 30%, evidence currency 25%, respectful family communication 15%.

units.title: Epidemiology, travel, zoonoses and special circumstances
objectives: Use an exposure calendar, geography, vectors, food/water, animal contact, migration and travel to generate (not prematurely close) a differential.
Distinguish endemic infection from travel-associated disease and account for changing epidemiology.
Select reference and public-health consultation resources for parasitic, vector-borne, mycobacterial and emerging infections.
topics: Domestic/international travel, immigrants/refugees, malaria, arboviruses, Lyme and other tick-borne illness, endemic fungi, zoonoses, TB/NTM, recreational exposures, trauma and outbreak/disaster contexts.
boardDomains: Prevention and containment of infectious diseases (8%)
units.casePractice: Fictional: child with fever after travel and one endemic exposure clue. Build an exposure timeline and list key test limitations. CDC DPDx adult cases can be used as laboratory-method examples only.
units.assessment: Exposure map + 3 differential branches. Rubric: exposure linkage 35%, diagnostic restraint 25%, source quality 20%, equity/cultural humility 20%.

units.title: Prevention, immunization, infection prevention and outbreak response
objectives: Apply a source-check workflow to routine, catch-up, medical-indication and special-situation immunization recommendations.
Explain transmission-based precautions, surveillance, outbreak case definitions, reportability, post-exposure response and school/childcare context.
Communicate vaccine evidence with respect and distinguish a special early dose from routine series completion.
topics: Active/passive immunization, live-vaccine cautions, immunocompromised children, maternal immunization, prophylaxis, IPC, outbreak investigations, vaccine hesitancy and public health.
boardDomains: Prevention and containment of infectious diseases (8%)
Core knowledge in scholarly activities and health equity (4%)
sourceUrls: CDC 2025 schedule page and notes (court-stay caveat)
units.casePractice: Fictional: school exposure notification to a child with altered immune function. Learner identifies information that must be checked with public-health authorities and current schedule notes.
units.assessment: One-page prevention plan with source/date stamps, contacts, limits and a family-facing plain-language summary. Rubric: current sources 40%, risk/precaution logic 25%, public-health coordination 20%, communication 15%.

units.title: Upper and lower respiratory tract infections
objectives: Compare common upper/lower respiratory syndrome patterns and assess complications and host-specific risks.
Interpret respiratory molecular panels carefully and explain when tests may not alter management.
Use current syndrome-specific guidelines and differentiate bacterial, viral, fungal and noninfectious alternatives.
topics: Sinusitis, otitis, pharyngitis, pertussis, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, empyema, aspiration, necrotizing/cavitary pneumonia; vaccine-preventable respiratory pathogens.
boardDomains: Prevention and containment of infectious diseases (8%)
units.casePractice: Fictional: child with cough and radiographic opacity; decide which history/exam/test features discriminate between likely categories and what panel positivity cannot establish alone.
units.assessment: Structured differential and test stewardship worksheet. Rubric: syndrome reasoning 35%, host/severity 25%, interpretation 20%, current sources 20%.

units.title: CNS, cardiovascular and endovascular infection
objectives: Build a time-sensitive differential for meningitis/encephalitis and recognize when prompt escalation is necessary.
Explain how microbiology and anatomic source inform endocarditis, myocarditis, pericarditis and septic thrombophlebitis assessments.
Distinguish infectious, postinfectious and inflammatory mimics.
topics: Bacterial/aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, brain/epidural abscess, toxin-mediated syndromes, endocarditis and device-associated/endovascular infection.
boardDomains: Central and peripheral nervous system infections (5%)
units.casePractice: Fictional: child with headache, fever and new focal neurologic finding. Build emergency differential and specimen/imaging question list without a treatment order.
units.assessment: Oral 8-minute diagnostic defense plus differential table. Rubric: threat recognition 30%, localization 25%, test reasoning 25%, limits/escalation 20%.

units.title: Bone, joint, skin, soft tissue, eye and lymphoid infection
objectives: Differentiate bone/joint and skin/soft tissue infection patterns from inflammatory, malignant and postinfectious mimics.
Identify the diagnostic value and limits of cultures/specimens, anatomy, host factors and source-control consultation.
Classify ocular/periorbital-orbital and lymphoid presentations for timely specialty coordination.
topics: Osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, discitis, cellulitis/abscess, pyomyositis/fasciitis, HSV/varicella lesions, ocular disease, lymphadenitis, fungal bone disease.
Kingella kingae diagnostic challenges in young children; culture and PCR detection differences; colonization versus invasive disease (historical lecture; use current guidance for care).
sourceUrls: PIDS/IDSA pediatric osteomyelitis guideline via IDSA guideline index
DPDx image library with license checks
units.casePractice: Fictional: child with limp and fever plus an epidemiologic clue. Compare pyogenic and fungal/inflammatory branches; state which data could prompt source-control evaluation.
units.assessment: Differential table with source-quality note; no copied clinical images. Rubric: differential breadth 30%, evidence 25%, source-control reasoning 20%, imaging/rights discipline 15%, clarity 10%.

units.title: GI, intra-abdominal, urinary, hepatic and reproductive infection
objectives: Interpret age/context, exposure and specimen quality in diarrheal, abdominal, UTI and hepatitis syndromes.
Distinguish infection from asymptomatic colonization and postinfectious/noninfectious conditions.
Use trauma-informed safeguarding and STI principles within appropriate clinical scope and local legal pathways.
topics: Gastroenteritis/colitis, appendicitis/peritonitis/abscess, UTI/renal abscess/asymptomatic bacteriuria, hepatitis/biliary abscess, STI and post-exposure evaluation.
sourceUrls: CDC DPDx cases and diagnostic references
units.casePractice: Fictional: child with abdominal symptoms and a contaminated specimen concern. Write what findings distinguish symptomatic infection from a positive test with no syndrome.
units.assessment: Case note and test-utilization critique; address consent/assent and appropriate safeguarding in the chosen fictional scenario. Rubric: syndrome/specimen 35%, differential 25%, ethics 20%, sources 20%.

units.title: Systemic infection, fever of unknown origin, recurrent and postinfectious conditions
objectives: Organize fever, bacteremia/sepsis, toxic shock and systemic fungal/viral syndromes by acuity, source and host.
Build an iterative fever-of-unknown-origin framework that includes infectious, inflammatory, malignant and other noninfectious etiologies.
Recognize recurrent infection patterns that warrant review for anatomic, immune, exposure, or ascertainment causes.
topics: Sepsis, ICU infection, bacteremia, fever without source, systemic fungi/viruses, HLH/MAS, Kawasaki disease, MIS-C/long COVID, periodic fevers, recurrent infections, postinfectious disease.
units.casePractice: Fictional: prolonged fever with episodic symptoms and a weakly positive serology. List infectious and noninfectious alternatives, assay limits, and a reassessment point.
units.assessment: Diagnostic time-line and prioritized re-evaluation plan; not a patient-care directive. Rubric: breadth 30%, evidence/test limits 25%, host context 20%, uncertainty 15%, clarity 10%.

units.title: Scholarly practice, quality, ethics and health equity
objectives: Critically appraise sensitivity/specificity, association/causation, bias, confounding, external validity and pediatric sample limitations.
Design a small, measurable stewardship or infection-prevention QI question with process/outcome/balancing measures.
Identify consent/assent, confidentiality, conflicts, structural barriers and equity implications in research and consultations.
topics: Clinical research, biostatistics, epidemiology, scholarly activity, publication review, QI/PDSA, professionalism, research ethics, health disparities and communication.
boardDomains: Core knowledge in scholarly activities and health equity (4%)
units.casePractice: Fictional: journal-club critique of a pediatric antimicrobial cohort study (provided article excerpts supplied by learner from lawfully accessible publication).
units.assessment: Structured appraisal + one-page PDSA proposal. Rubric: methods 35%, clinical relevance 20%, ethical/equity design 20%, measurable QI 15%, writing 10%.

assignment.title: Integrated pediatric ID consult, evidence appraisal and stewardship portfolio
tasks: Write a fictional 1–2 page consultation formulation with timeline, host factors, ranked differential and discriminating evidence; no real patient information.
Critically appraise one lawfully accessible pediatric ID primary study or guideline using design, bias, outcome, external validity and equity prompts.
Prepare a one-page stewardship/prevention action proposal with process, outcome and balancing measures; distinguish local quality improvement from research that requires review.
Deliver an 8-minute recorded or live oral defense using linked sources and no patient images unless separately licensed and de-identified.
assignment.rightsAndSafety: Use fictional scenarios by default. For genuine educational cases, use the source institution’s public case link only, follow the source’s rights rules, do not copy or rehost patient records or imagery, and obtain any required permission. This assignment is not clinical credentialing.

assessment.format: 10 original source-cited multiple-choice questions plus case-based written/oral portfolio and unit formative tasks.
assessment.passingStandard: No validated cut score. For self-study, review rationales and current source material after each response; this assessment is not an official board exam, readiness predictor or clinical competency evaluation.
assessment.questionRights: All questions are newly authored for this course from public blueprint/guideline evidence; none are copied from ABP or proprietary question banks.

studyHours.type: transparent planning estimate, not measured instructional time
studyHours.assumptions: Plan: 36-hour target recorded course floor (only 5.0958 ready now); about 54 hours of reading/guideline comparison; 32 hours in cases/assignments; 12 hours retrieval practice and reflection; 10 hours scholarly-appraisal/QI work. Study plan is not an actual workload measurement and source-update time may vary.

mapping.name: Pediatric Infectious Diseases Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official Boston Children’s GME page describes a categorical three-year clinical physician fellowship, ACGME-accredited; year one focused on clinical training and years two/three research-focused. Public clinical page reports first-year inpatient service about eight months including about six months at BCH, one month adult General ID at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and half-month pediatric ID at Boston Medical Center; plus microbiology/virology (one month), infection prevention/stewardship (half-month), outpatient clinics and conferences. Years two/three have at least 80% protected research time with ongoing but limited consultations. These are the public description, not a guarantee of current exact rotations or didactic hours.

coveredTopics: Antibacterial, antiviral, antifungal and antiparasitic principles; allergy labels; therapeutic monitoring; narrow-spectrum choices; audit/feedback; source control.

unitMap.text: Infections in immunocompromised hosts and device/transplant settings
coveredTopics: Primary and acquired immunodeficiency, central line/device and post-surgical infection, donor-derived risk, transplant-associated infection, malignancy and febrile neutropenia, cystic fibrosis.

unitMap.text: Fetus, neonate and febrile young infant
coveredTopics: Congenital CMV, syphilis, HIV and other congenital infection; neonatal HSV, perinatal exposure, sepsis/meningitis; febrile infant evidence and pathophysiology.

unitMap.text: Epidemiology, travel, zoonoses and special circumstances
coveredTopics: Domestic/international travel, immigrants/refugees, malaria, arboviruses, Lyme and other tick-borne illness, endemic fungi, zoonoses, TB/NTM, recreational exposures, trauma and outbreak/disaster contexts.

unitMap.text: Prevention, immunization, infection prevention and outbreak response

unitMap.text: CNS, cardiovascular and endovascular infection
coveredTopics: Bacterial/aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, brain/epidural abscess, toxin-mediated syndromes, endocarditis and device-associated/endovascular infection.

coveredTopics: Osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, discitis, cellulitis/abscess, pyomyositis/fasciitis, HSV/varicella lesions, ocular disease, lymphadenitis, fungal bone disease.
Kingella kingae diagnostic challenges in young children; culture and PCR detection differences; colonization versus invasive disease (historical lecture; use current guidance for care).

unitMap.text: GI, intra-abdominal, urinary, hepatic and reproductive infection

coveredTopics: Sepsis, ICU infection, bacteremia, fever without source, systemic fungi/viruses, HLH/MAS, Kawasaki disease, MIS-C/long COVID, periodic fevers, recurrent infections, postinfectious disease.

unitMap.text: Scholarly practice, quality, ethics and health equity
coveredTopics: Clinical research, biostatistics, epidemiology, scholarly activity, publication review, QI/PDSA, professionalism, research ethics, health disparities and communication.

topicGaps: Verified accessible free specialty-recording hours total 5.9292, leaving a 30.0708-hour gap against the 36-hour floor. The 58:24 general/adult CDC transplant recording remains supplementary and excluded from specialty hours. No scripted episode or planned target minutes count as ready media.

Public free-recording coverage remains thin or absent for ocular, reproductive, lymphoid, urinary/hepatobiliary and GI infection; CNS/endovascular disease; mycobacterial, fungal and parasitic diagnostics beyond selected lectures; detailed pediatric antimicrobial PK/PD; and scholarship/health equity. Four original source-grounded episodes are scripted, not rendered, and cannot be counted as hours.

A directly opened UCLA Pediatric Grand Rounds video provides one new 50:00 specialty recording for bone/joint and microbiology coverage. The 2016 content is historical. Other candidate pages examined for refugee/travel and Kawasaki lectures showed “Video unavailable” in the rendered player; despite metadata/runtime text, they were excluded as inaccessible. CDC’s directly linked malaria RDT recording page also rendered “Video unavailable” and was excluded.

Existing 24-item clip-plan targets total 1,872 planned minutes (31.2 target-hours), a production plan only—not rendered/verified media. This plan does not close the 30.0708-hour gap; output length must be probed and playback checked after production.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — Pediatric Infectious Diseases subspecialty certification examination
medical.boardStatus: Separate ABP pediatric infectious diseases subspecialty certifying examination exists. The ABP’s current public page requires three years full-time broad-based pediatric ID fellowship training in a qualifying ACGME- or RCPSC-accredited program plus general criteria, scholarly activity verification, and passing the examination. No separate ABIM/AOBIM pediatric-ID exam identified. The one-month adult ID rotation at BIDMC is a rotation, not evidence of an adult board track.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not grant ABP eligibility or certification. Eligibility is individual, governed by current ABP rules, qualifying prerequisite general pediatrics certification/training, accredited fellowship training and other requirements; candidates must confirm directly with ABP. No pass guarantee.

officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Infectious Diseases Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official Boston Children’s GME page describes a categorical three-year clinical physician fellowship, ACGME-accredited; year one focused on clinical training and years two/three research-focused. Public clinical page reports first-year inpatient service about eight months including about six months at BCH, one month adult General ID at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and half-month pediatric ID at Boston Medical Center; plus microbiology/virology (one month), infection prevention/stewardship (half-month), outpatient clinics and conferences. Years two/three have at least 80% protected research time with ongoing but limited consultations. These are the public description, not a guarantee of current exact rotations or didactic hours.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet item names one actual Harvard-affiliated physician fellowship at Boston Children’s Hospital. Preserve this institutional variant exactly. The programme page says the program encourages applications from people interested in combined Internal Medicine-Pediatrics ID and combined pediatric subspecialty training, but it does not describe a specific integrated combined track or guarantee a position; do not list those as separate offerings. PIDS describes an optional additional pediatric transplant/ICH ID fellowship as non-ACGME and notes Boston’s opportunity is not advertised and is not offered every year; that is a post-fellowship supplement, not a second core PID program or separate ABP certificate. Pediatric ID is a real physician subspecialty, not a generic directory label, non-physician course or research-only postdoctoral position. No additional Harvard/Johns Hopkins offering is attributed to this single packet without a verified official program page.
sourceCaveats: Boston Children’s site is the official programme source and describes ACGME accreditation; ACGME requirements and ABP certification blueprint are distinct from the site’s public educational description. Confirm ongoing accreditation/rotations directly before relying on them.
ABP content outline effective Oct. 1, 2025: weights are approximate; actual exam versions may vary. Eligibility/certification criteria can change without notice.

CDC immunization schedule was checked on 2026-10-07; the page stated that the current schedule was the July 2, 2025 schedule because of a March 2026 court order. Re-open current CDC/ACIP and local public-health sources before clinical use.
NIH pediatric HIV OI webpage reported updates through Apr. 23, 2026 and is dynamically updated; follow the current live section, not saved recommendations.

Recorded content varies in date and scope. A research discussion, society webinar, educational lecture and guideline have different authority. Do not convert older slides/video into current treatment protocol.

The only current packet programme variant assigned here is Boston Children’s Hospital. Boston’s encouragement of combined interests is not evidence of a distinct integrated position; optional transplant/ICH extra training is reported by PIDS as non-ACGME and not offered each year.

No institutional patient case volumes, trainee eligibility beyond published criteria, guaranteed board outcome, individual diagnosis/treatment advice or procedural competence claims are made. No patient record/image was copied into these files.
Human clinical review is not performed. Independent self-study confers no institutional affiliation, accredited training, licensure, supervised competence, board eligibility or certification.
