topicGaps: Verified accessible free specialty-recording hours total 5.9292, leaving a 30.0708-hour gap against the 36-hour floor. The 58:24 general/adult CDC transplant recording remains supplementary and excluded from specialty hours. No scripted episode or planned target minutes count as ready media.

Public free-recording coverage remains thin or absent for ocular, reproductive, lymphoid, urinary/hepatobiliary and GI infection; CNS/endovascular disease; mycobacterial, fungal and parasitic diagnostics beyond selected lectures; detailed pediatric antimicrobial PK/PD; and scholarship/health equity. Four original source-grounded episodes are scripted, not rendered, and cannot be counted as hours.

A directly opened UCLA Pediatric Grand Rounds video provides one new 50:00 specialty recording for bone/joint and microbiology coverage. The 2016 content is historical. Other candidate pages examined for refugee/travel and Kawasaki lectures showed “Video unavailable” in the rendered player; despite metadata/runtime text, they were excluded as inaccessible. CDC’s directly linked malaria RDT recording page also rendered “Video unavailable” and was excluded.

Existing 24-item clip-plan targets total 1,872 planned minutes (31.2 target-hours), a production plan only—not rendered/verified media. This plan does not close the 30.0708-hour gap; output length must be probed and playback checked after production.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 9-year-old with acute leukemia develops fever during profound neutropenia. A blood culture later reports a Gram-negative bacillus with a resistance phenotype not covered by the original empiric choice. Which is the best next learning-principle response?

options.text: Assume the organism is susceptible because the child is receiving broad-spectrum therapy.
Integrate current clinical status, isolate identification/susceptibilities, local guidance, source control and specialist/team input; reassess empiric coverage against the actual evidence.
Add multiple agents without reviewing cultures or toxicity.
Use adult-only recommendations without checking age, organism or local resistance data.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A high-risk host requires prompt, iterative, team-based review of culture, susceptibility and clinical severity. The task is reasoning, not a treatment order. The ABP outline includes high-risk hosts, microbiology and stewardship; BCH notes this host group in actual clinical training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A stable child has cough, a positive broad respiratory molecular panel for a virus, and no other evidence of bacterial disease. What is the most important interpretation?

options.text: A positive panel proves the virus explains every symptom and rules out all coinfection.
Interpret the result with syndrome, timing, host, specimen and pretest probability; panel detection may not alone establish causality or change management.
Treat every detected organism.
Repeat the panel daily until negative.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Diagnostic stewardship includes test indication, interpretation, and avoiding low-value repeated or broad-panel testing; a detected nucleic acid is not always causal proof.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reviews a public CDC parasite image and wants to paste it into a course handout. Which is appropriate?

options.text: All images on any free website are free to republish.
Check the CDC page-specific copyright/permission statement; CDC DPDx identifies most material as public domain but specifies named copyrighted images, and citations are still required.
Copy it if patient identifiers are absent.
Remove the image credit to avoid confusion.

practiceQuestions.rationale: DPDx states most material is public domain but lists specific copyrighted images; free view and permission to rehost are not equivalent.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner uses an early measles vaccination dose for an infant under 12 months as if it replaced the later routine series. Which response best matches responsible curriculum practice?

options.text: It always replaces the routine doses.
Confirm current ACIP/CDC outbreak and travel guidance; an early dose in a special context does not automatically replace later age-appropriate routine doses.
Use a general podcast instead of checking the current schedule.
Do not vaccinate any infant under 12 months.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current schedule and special indications must be consulted; PIDS interview discussion cannot supersede current CDC schedule/health-department instructions, and its transcript states early vaccine dose does not replace routine two doses.

practiceQuestions.stem: A febrile infant evidence discussion reports a small observational cohort. Which inference is justified?

options.text: A small retrospective cohort proves a strategy is safe for every infant.
The study can inform a question but sample, selection, age range, outcomes and generalizability limit inference; use the current age-specific guideline and clinical supervision.
All neonates should receive the same regimen.
A video replaces institutional pathway review.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Research updates are not clinical practice guidelines; external validity and design matter, especially in age-stratified high-risk patients.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees coccidioidomycosis discussed in children and decides that any child with fever and bone pain has disseminated disease. What reasoning correction is best?

options.text: A short society interview establishes the diagnosis.
Treat geography/exposure and clinical pattern as differential inputs, seek fit-for-purpose tests, and avoid extrapolating a research discussion to diagnosis or treatment.
All bone pain is fungal disease.
Ignore geographic epidemiology.

practiceQuestions.rationale: An epidemiologic clue informs but does not determine diagnosis. PIDS clip discusses a study and rising burden; current disease evaluation requires primary sources and supervised care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric ID fellow is making a transplant-related study plan from Boston Children’s public page. Which is accurately represented?

options.text: All three years are inpatient service.
Year one is predominantly clinical, while years two and three are research-focused with at least 80% protected research time; clinical work continues but is limited.
The program is a research-only postdoc.
Every graduate automatically receives ABP certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The program page states a three-year categorical clinical physician fellowship, year one clinical, years two/three research with at least 80% protected research time; training makes candidate eligible only if board rules met and the exam is passed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is asked whether Boston Children’s offers a separately accredited pediatric transplant-ID fellowship every year. What is best supported by the public evidence reviewed?

options.text: Yes, the standard three-year ACGME fellowship includes a separate extra year for all fellows.
No, PIDS lists optional additional non-ACGME transplant/ICH fellowships and notes BCH opportunity is not advertised and not offered every year; inquire with program for current details.
The ABP grants transplant-ID board certification.
There is a guaranteed combined med-peds track.

practiceQuestions.rationale: PIDS explicitly labels these as additional, non-ACGME opportunities and gives a year-to-year availability caveat. BCH encourages combined interests but its web page does not establish a separate integrated track or guaranteed opening.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which board relationship applies to the packet’s pediatric infectious diseases physician fellowship?

options.text: The ABIM is the sole certifying board.
The ABP offers a pediatric infectious diseases subspecialty certifying exam; eligible applicants must meet prerequisite training and additional ABP conditions.
There is no separate board examination.
Course completion alone guarantees ABP certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP publishes a PID subspecialty certification page and current content outline. The fellowship site says training meets the training requirement to take the examination, not that the independent course grants eligibility or certification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A team evaluates a stewardship feedback intervention in complex children hospitalized with pneumonia. Which plan best supports credible QI/research learning?

options.text: Measure prescribing alone and claim causation from any change.
Predefine process/outcome/balancing measures, assess population and confounders, monitor unintended effects, and distinguish local QI from generalizable research.
Use number of lectures watched as the patient outcome.
Collect identifiable clinical records in a personal course folder.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP domain 22 includes research design, bias, ethics, QI and equity; stewardship measures should avoid overclaiming and protect patient privacy.

title: Pediatric Infectious Diseases Fellowships
prerequisites: Medical-school-level foundations in microbiology, immunology, pharmacology, pediatrics, epidemiology, and evidence appraisal

objectives: Construct age- and host-aware infectious differential diagnoses and identify time-critical risks without over-interpreting a single finding.

Interpret evidence and communicate diagnostic uncertainty, harms, follow-up, and equity considerations.
Map study to the broad topics in the ABP Pediatric Infectious Diseases content outline without claiming a verbatim or weighted official blueprint mapping.

topicGaps: Pediatric diagnostics/microbiology across pathogens; clinical reasoning in high-risk hosts; congenital/perinatal infection; immunization and immunocompromised-host schedules; respiratory, CNS, invasive/endovascular, bone/joint, urinary, fungal and parasitic syndromes remain without topic-specific verified recordings in this ledger.

New Seattle Children's Grand Rounds add pediatric TB program systems/equity/referral, pediatric antimicrobial stewardship and IV-to-oral/OPAT reasoning, and resource-constrained pediatric sepsis context. They are not a comprehensive course and do not close the 32.078-hour video gap.
Most source-backed unit instruction remains readings and scripted episodes/plans, not recordings. No rendering, recording or upload is claimed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — Pediatric Infectious Diseases subspecialty certification examination
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABP subspecialty certifying examination exists. The ABP page reviewed 2025-11-25 requires three years of full-time broad-based fellowship in an ACGME-accredited U.S. or RCPSC-accredited Canadian program, prior general pediatrics certification criteria, training verification, scholarly activity, and passing the subspecialty exam. PIDS reports the examination is offered every other year in November of odd years; verify current ABP dates and eligibility directly.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course confers no board eligibility. Eligibility depends on board rules, accredited supervised training, prior certification, program verification and scholarly work. The ABP warns its criteria may change.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Children's Center
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Infectious Diseases Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page calls it a three-year ACGME-accredited physician fellowship designed for pediatric ID board certification; 12 months clinical ID training, with subsequent two years predominantly research and 18 months protected research time. Lists microbial pathogenesis, virology, parasitology, immunobiology, vaccinology, hospital epidemiology, antimicrobial stewardship and international health. It does not publish a detailed rotation calendar, case numbers or lecture-hour inventory. The associated fellowship directory separately calls the site The Johns Hopkins Hospital and labels it ACGME Accredited.

officialProgrammes.name: Four-year combined pediatric-adult infectious diseases fellowship track (as described on Pediatric Infectious Diseases Fellowship page)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Hopkins says it also accepts candidates interested in a four-year combined pediatric-adult fellowship in combination with its Adult Infectious Diseases Fellowship. This is a distinct institutional combined track, not a separate pediatric-only curriculum or board. Do not infer eligibility for both boards from this listing; ABP and ABIM requirements apply independently and were not fully investigated here.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The supplied input names one physician subspecialty and one Hopkins program. Its official page distinguishes ACGME-accredited clinical fellowship from the associated research training opportunities. The combined pediatric-adult option is preserved as an institutional variant. Hopkins' general directory is a listing, not a curriculum. No Harvard offering was named in this item's packet or verified in this focused scope. No separate non-physician credential or research-only fellowship is included. Hopkins notes research is a major component, but the core offering remains a clinical physician fellowship.
sourceCaveats: Institution and board claims are based on public pages accessed on 2026-10-07. Programme pages are not a substitute for current application/eligibility verification.

The pediatric immunization page reports a legally stayed 2026 schedule revision and says the July 2, 2025 schedule is currently posted. This is a time-sensitive legal/policy qualifier; recheck CDC and controlling court status immediately before clinical use.

The ABP's 2025 practice analysis abstract reports structure and selected directional changes but does not expose the full official content outline or domain weights. Course domains are a transparent educational crosswalk, not exact weighted board blueprint replication.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-aged child has acute sore throat with cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness and conjunctivitis. Under CDC guidance, what is the best next testing approach for group A streptococcal pharyngitis?

options.text: Routine rapid antigen test because every sore throat requires GAS testing.
Clear viral symptoms generally mean GAS testing is not needed.
Treat presumptively for GAS without testing.
Obtain blood culture.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC states clear viral symptoms suggest viral pharyngitis and do not require GAS testing; avoiding unnecessary testing and antibiotics is appropriate stewardship.

practiceQuestions.stem: A symptomatic 8-year-old without clear viral symptoms has a negative rapid antigen detection test for GAS. Which follow-up is recommended by CDC?

options.text: No additional test is ever indicated after a negative rapid test.
Back up the negative rapid test with throat culture and have a mechanism to contact the family if positive.
Obtain serum antistreptolysin O immediately to diagnose acute pharyngitis.
Treat every negative rapid test with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

practiceQuestions.rationale: For symptomatic children aged 3 years or older, CDC advises confirming a negative RADT with throat culture and following up a positive culture.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn is being evaluated for congenital CMV. Which test/timing statement best aligns with CDC guidance?

options.text: IgM alone at 4 months definitively establishes congenital infection.
PCR testing of saliva, with urine confirmation, should be performed within 2–3 weeks after birth to distinguish congenital from postnatal infection.
Any positive urine PCR at 6 months proves congenital infection.
Routine prenatal maternal screening is recommended for all pregnancies.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC says PCR on saliva is preferred with urine confirmation and testing should occur within 2–3 weeks; later testing cannot distinguish congenital from postnatal infection. Antibody testing does not diagnose congenital CMV.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 4-year-old had close household exposure to an adult with TB. The first infection test is negative, but it was obtained shortly after exposure. What is the key reasoning step?

options.text: A negative early test rules out infection and disease.

Assess for TB disease and consult pediatric TB/public-health expertise; CDC describes window prophylaxis for exposed children under five even with an early negative test, with repeat testing 8–10 weeks after last exposure.
Repeat only if symptoms develop years later.
Assume active TB and prescribe a regimen without evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC guidance emphasizes ruling out TB disease and describes window prophylaxis and repeat testing for young children; management should involve expert advice and current guidelines.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 6-year-old has a history of BCG vaccination and requires TB infection testing. What does CDC recommend?

options.text: An IGRA is recommended for children aged 5 years or older who received BCG, because BCG does not affect the blood test.
BCG invalidates all TB testing.
Use antibody testing for TB.
Interpret the skin test differently solely because BCG was given.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC recommends a TB blood test for children at least five years old who have received BCG; IGRA is not affected by BCG. The skin test is interpreted using the same risk-based criteria regardless of BCG history.

practiceQuestions.stem: A positive TB infection test is obtained in a child. Which principle is essential before classifying the child as having latent TB infection or starting preventive treatment?

options.text: Latent infection can be diagnosed from the positive test alone.
Evaluate for TB disease; CDC states disease must be excluded before latent infection treatment begins.
A negative sputum test always excludes pediatric TB disease.
No chest radiograph is ever part of evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC defines LTBI in the absence of evidence of disease after evaluation and stresses ensuring TB disease is absent before LTBI treatment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician needs to review current child immunization recommendations in October 2026. What is the safest approach based on CDC's schedule page reviewed for this curriculum?

options.text: Use any older schedule without checking version.
Use the live CDC page and verify its legal/policy notice and current schedule version; that page stated the July 2, 2025 schedule was currently posted after a March 2026 court stay.
Assume the schedule never changes.
Replace national guidance with an unverified social-media infographic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CDC page included a time-sensitive notice that the July 2, 2025 schedule was the current posted schedule because of a court stay. Learners must check the live source and governing status at point of use.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner finds a short Hopkins directory entry labeled ACGME Accredited and a separate detailed fellowship page. Which statement correctly distinguishes these sources?

options.text: The directory alone establishes every rotation and didactic hour.

The directory is a listing/accreditation label; detailed public program description separately reports three years, 12 clinical months and protected research time, while a detailed rotation calendar is not published there.
The directory is the ABP certification rule.
The listing proves a 4-year combined track is a separate board.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins' directory gives location, accreditation label and duration; the institutional program page gives the clinical/research balance and combined track note. Accreditation and public listing do not establish a full curriculum or board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes ABP certification after pediatric ID fellowship?

options.text: Independent self-study alone makes a learner eligible.

The ABP describes a separate Pediatric Infectious Diseases certifying examination and requires specified accredited training, general eligibility, verified training, scholarly activity and passing the exam.
There is no separate pediatric ID board examination.
A combined institutional track automatically guarantees two board credentials.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABP pediatric ID page describes training requirements and a subspecialty certifying examination. The PIDS guide reports the exam is offered every other year, but current dates and eligibility must be verified directly with ABP.

options.text: It publishes all exact domain percentages in the accessible summary.
It reports a final outline of 22 domains and 196 subdomains and directional changes in selected areas; this course does not claim to reproduce the full weighted outline.
It establishes a validated pass guarantee for this course.
It proves lectures replace supervised clinical training.

title: Pediatric Nephrology Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (ACGME-accredited subspecialty pathway; separate board certification exists through ABP)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Physician-level completion of pediatrics residency (or other current ABP-approved prerequisite route); this self-study does not substitute for it.
Advanced postgraduate learners with renal physiology, fluid/electrolyte, acid-base, pediatric assessment, evidence appraisal and general pediatrics knowledge.
Ability to read a clinical vignette and basic urine/kidney-function data; no independent diagnostic/procedural competence is implied.
objectives: Map learning to all 12 ABP Pediatric Nephrology examination content domains current from March 15, 2026, while recognizing the blueprint is not a complete curriculum.
Construct source-cited pediatric renal differentials from developmental context, clinical trajectory, laboratory data, urine and imaging reports.
Explain major pediatric renal syndrome mechanisms, diagnostic uncertainties and current guideline scope without issuing patient-specific treatment orders.
Compare kidney replacement therapy and transplant domains conceptually and recognize when supervised multidisciplinary decisions are essential.
Appraise studies, guideline dates, evidence strength, equity, ethics and privacy in pediatric nephrology.
Use board-cognitive retrieval, single-best-answer analysis and rationales without implying validated readiness or a passing prediction.

assignment.title: Pediatric renal reasoning and evidence appraisal portfolio
assignment.instructions: Using only the fictional vignettes supplied within this independent course, prepare (1) a 1,500–2,000 word source-cited reasoning memo, (2) a one-page differential/data-gap matrix, and (3) an 8-minute oral defense. For each vignette distinguish facts, interpretation and unknowns; map relevant ABP domain(s); cite current primary guidance; identify a safe need for supervised clinical evaluation when appropriate. Do not include identifiable patient information, individualized prescriptions, procedure instructions, or downloaded/reproduced diagnostic images. The published nephrotic-syndrome case link may be critically appraised but is not current treatment guidance.

rubric.excellent: Accurately represents available information, considers plausible alternatives and identifies discriminating missing data without premature diagnostic certainty.
Uses current, authoritative sources, dates them and maps to ABP domains without claiming the outline is a complete curriculum.
Separates education from patient care, flags urgent/supervised needs and avoids prescription/procedural overreach.
Uses fictional or lawfully linked de-identified educational material, protects privacy, and considers developmental/family context.
Delivers a concise, logically structured oral and written explanation with citations.

assignment.passingGuidance: Suggested formative threshold only; no validated competency measure, board-readiness score or clinical authorization.

assessment.format: 10 original board-cognitive single-best-answer practice questions with rationales; unit retrieval exercises; case/source appraisal; final portfolio and oral defense. Questions are original, not ABP exam content.
assessment.standard: Formative educational scoring only. Not validated for predicting examination performance, certification, eligibility, clinical competency or procedural competence.

unitMap.text: Developmental renal physiology, fetal/neonatal nephrology and fluid homeostasis
coveredTopics: Embryology; neonatal renal circulation; concentrating ability; sodium/water; potassium, calcium/phosphate and magnesium; acid-base; tubular disorders.

unitMap.text: Core diagnostics: urine, filtration, imaging, pathology and genetics
coveredTopics: Urinalysis; protein quantification; eGFR; kidney/bladder ultrasound; radionuclide/other imaging concepts; biopsy indications/risks/pathology; genetic testing.

unitMap.text: Glomerular syndromes and nephrotic syndrome
coveredTopics: Proteinuria/hematuria; congenital/infantile NS; minimal change, FSGS; IgA/C3/MPGN; postinfectious GN; lupus/vasculitis/anti-GBM; TMA; COL4A disease.

unitMap.text: Acute kidney injury and acute kidney replacement therapy
coveredTopics: AKI definitions/trends; sepsis, HUS, nephrotoxins, glomerular causes; obstruction; AKI complications; acute intermittent HD, PD and continuous therapies.

unitMap.text: Congenital, structural, cystic and tubulointerstitial disease
coveredTopics: Hydronephrosis/obstruction; dysplasia/hypoplasia; solitary kidney/MCDK; VUR; ADPKD/ARPKD; ciliopathies; tubulointerstitial nephritis.

unitMap.text: Urinary tract, micturition, infection, stones and renal masses
coveredTopics: Micturition and bladder dysfunction; UTI; reflux; urolithiasis (calcium, uric acid, cystine, oxalate, struvite); renal masses.

unitMap.text: Pediatric blood pressure and hypertension
coveredTopics: Measurement technique; normal/elevated BP and hypertension; white-coat/masked patterns; renal/renovascular and systemic causes; ABPM; long-term risk.

unitMap.text: Chronic kidney disease, growth and systemic complications
coveredTopics: CKD progression; growth/nutrition; anemia; CKD-MBD; acid-base/electrolytes; cardiovascular, neurocognitive, immune and psychosocial sequelae; medications.

unitMap.text: Maintenance dialysis and kidney replacement planning
coveredTopics: Hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis; access; prescription/adequacy concepts; complications; school and family life; transition and conservative options.

unitMap.text: Pediatric kidney transplantation
coveredTopics: HLA/crossmatch concepts; living/deceased donor; ethics/equity; induction/maintenance immunosuppression; rejection; recurrent/de novo disease; infection/PTLD; adherence and transition.

unitMap.text: Research methods, epidemiology, scholarship and quality improvement
coveredTopics: Biostatistics; epidemiology; trials/cohorts/registries; evidence grading; pediatric research protections; QI measures and balancing measures.

unitMap.text: Integrated board-style reasoning, patient safety and transition
coveredTopics: Mixed ABP blueprint cases; handoffs; adolescent transition; communication; equity; ethics; safety/QI; exam blueprint versus curriculum distinction.

topicGaps: One free public recording with verified duration supports kidney-genomics diagnostic teaching in part: 53:16 (0.8878 hours); total verified external specialty time is 0.8878 hours and the 36-hour target remains short by 35.1122 hours.

The sole recording maps to Units 2 and 5, but its stated objectives are limited to sequencing utility/yield, clinical impact and multidisciplinary genetics workflow; it does not cover complete diagnostics, biopsy, imaging, or structural/cystic disease.

No duration-verified, freely accessible recordings were established in this evidence set for fetal/neonatal physiology; fluid, electrolyte or acid-base disorders; comprehensive urine/GFR/imaging/biopsy diagnostics; glomerular disease; AKI or acute dialysis; CAKUT or tubulointerstitial disease; urinary tract infection, micturition, stones or masses; pediatric blood pressure; CKD complications; maintenance dialysis; transplantation; or scholarly skills.

Four full original scripts are authored in the separate episode file: blueprint-oriented reasoning, genetic diagnostic reasoning, AKI reasoning, and longitudinal CKD synthesis. They are scripted and unrendered, contribute zero verified media hours, and do not close the 36-hour gap.
The 72 original 30-minute clip entries remain production plans only (nominal planned total 36 hours); target minutes are not observed runtime, completed lectures, or verified hours.
The pre-existing YouTube leads and the IPNA Vimeo candidate remain unverified and uncounted; the ASPN recordings page states that member webinars and recordings are available for ASPN members.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (ACGME-accredited subspecialty pathway; separate board certification exists through ABP)
boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — Pediatric Nephrology subspecialty certifying examination
American Board of Pediatrics — General Pediatrics certification (prior board pathway context; not a second pediatric nephrology board examination)
medical.boardStatus: The ABP recognizes Pediatric Nephrology as a subspecialty certification and requires passage of a subspecialty certifying examination after applicable eligibility requirements. The ABP Pediatric Nephrology SITE is an in-training assessment, not a separate board certification. ACGME accreditation is programme accreditation, not individual certification. No distinct separate institutional or pediatric nephrology board exam beyond ABP was identified.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABP public criteria (page last updated 2025-11-25) require three years full-time broad-based fellowship training in pediatric nephrology in an ACGME-accredited U.S. or RCPSC-accredited Canadian training program, other ABP general criteria, satisfactory final program-director evaluation including clinical competence/professionalism and scholarship, and a passed ABP subspecialty certifying exam. Current criteria can change and individual eligibility must be confirmed with ABP. This independent self-study course confers no eligibility, certification or licensure.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Children’s Center
officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Nephrology Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The supplied official listing states ACGME Accredited and three years; it reports 52 weeks over the three years treating in/outpatients including ICU kidney replacement therapies, epidemiology master’s coursework and optional basic-science research. The current Children’s Center page separately describes longitudinal inpatient, continuity clinic, HD/PD/transplant, MHS clinical epidemiology, QI, elective offerings and weekly didactics/pathology/journal clubs/board review. Public description is not a full syllabus or independent ADS verification.

officialProgrammes.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital / Harvard Medical School
officialProgrammes.name: Division of Nephrology Fellowship Training Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official programme page describes a three-year fellowship with 12 months intensive clinical and 24 months research training, inpatient/consult, transplant and dialysis/general clinic work, pathology and uroradiology exposure, and says it meets ACGME Pediatric Nephrology sub-board requirements. The published division-level page is not a private trainee schedule, does not establish an individual fellow’s case volume or independent current ADS status.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet variants are preserved exactly in substance: Johns Hopkins Pediatric Nephrology Fellowship and Boston Children’s Hospital Division of Nephrology Fellowship Training Program (Harvard Medical School). Both describe actual physician clinical subspecialty fellowship offerings; Hopkins official listing explicitly reports ACGME accreditation; BCH page describes its programme as ACGME accredited/meeting ABP-nephrology requirements. ACGME 2026 requirements index is current as of July 1, 2026; individual program accreditation status was not separately checked in ADS. The Johns Hopkins general fellowship directory is a listing page, not a generic specialty nor a different combined programme. The optional basic-science research track at Johns Hopkins and BCH’s research years are components of clinical physician fellowships, not stand-alone non-physician or research-only tracks. No combined internal medicine-pediatrics nephrology programme or separate nephrology board was established for this item.
sourceCaveats: Current clinical guideline basis includes KDIGO 2025 pediatric nephrotic syndrome recommendations; check living guidelines, updates, jurisdiction-specific standards and specialist judgment before any clinical use.
ABP content outline effective March 15, 2026 is an exam blueprint only and explicitly not a curriculum or study guide.
AAP pediatric blood-pressure guidance cited is 2017; confirm any later update before application.
The NIH NIDDK overview was last reviewed August 2022.

Stateless fetch of the ACGME 2026 pediatric-nephrology PDF failed to extract text; the official Pediatrics index confirms the item/effective date and direct URL. Individual site accreditation was not verified in the public ADS finder.

The linked 2020 case report is included for critique only: publication narrative has inconsistencies and potentially outdated recommendations; formal de-identification authorization and figure reuse permission were not confirmed. Do not copy text/images or treat it as a protocol.

Clinical review by a human clinician was not performed. Independent education is unaffiliated with Johns Hopkins, Harvard, Boston Children’s Hospital, ABP or ACGME and does not replace accredited training, supervised care or licensure.

topicGaps: One free public recording with verified duration supports kidney-genomics diagnostic teaching in part: 53:16 (0.8878 hours); total verified external specialty time is 0.8878 hours and the 36-hour target remains short by 35.1122 hours.

The sole recording maps to Units 2 and 5, but its stated objectives are limited to sequencing utility/yield, clinical impact and multidisciplinary genetics workflow; it does not cover complete diagnostics, biopsy, imaging, or structural/cystic disease.

No duration-verified, freely accessible recordings were established in this evidence set for fetal/neonatal physiology; fluid, electrolyte or acid-base disorders; comprehensive urine/GFR/imaging/biopsy diagnostics; glomerular disease; AKI or acute dialysis; CAKUT or tubulointerstitial disease; urinary tract infection, micturition, stones or masses; pediatric blood pressure; CKD complications; maintenance dialysis; transplantation; or scholarly skills.

Four full original scripts are authored in the separate episode file: blueprint-oriented reasoning, genetic diagnostic reasoning, AKI reasoning, and longitudinal CKD synthesis. They are scripted and unrendered, contribute zero verified media hours, and do not close the 36-hour gap.
The 72 original 30-minute clip entries remain production plans only (nominal planned total 36 hours); target minutes are not observed runtime, completed lectures, or verified hours.
The pre-existing YouTube leads and the IPNA Vimeo candidate remain unverified and uncounted; the ASPN recordings page states that member webinars and recordings are available for ASPN members.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional preschool child has edema, clearly nephrotic-range proteinuria and low serum albumin. Which conclusion is best supported by these findings alone?

options.text: The nephrotic syndrome phenotype is present; etiology and histology are not established by this information alone.
Minimal change disease is proven.
Steroid resistance is established.
Thrombotic microangiopathy is proven.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The clinical phenotype can be recognized from proteinuria plus hypoalbuminemia/edema, but the data do not establish histology, response category or etiology. Apply the current KDIGO pediatric guideline and the full clinical context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with gross hematuria has low C3 after a recent infection. Which reasoning step is most defensible?

options.text: Use the complement result and timing to prioritize a post-infectious glomerular process, while retaining a differential and arranging context-appropriate follow-up.
Conclude that the case is biopsy-proven post-infectious GN.
Exclude glomerular disease because hematuria is visible.
Diagnose IgA nephropathy solely from gross hematuria.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Low complement and temporal context can support a differential but do not independently prove etiology. The learner must integrate urine, renal function, BP, serology and course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A hospitalized child develops rising creatinine and reduced urine output. Which initial framework best avoids premature closure?

options.text: Assess trajectory and volume/perfusion context, medicines/exposures, urine findings and possible obstruction, while evaluating complications.
Assume prerenal azotemia if there was any vomiting.
Use one urine index as a definitive discriminator in every child.
Wait for a second abnormal creatinine before considering AKI.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric AKI reasoning integrates timing, baseline, hemodynamics, exposures, urine and obstruction. No single clue or index resolves every case; assess complications and escalate appropriately.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with elevated office blood pressure on repeated visits has uncertainty about the out-of-office phenotype. Which test is specifically useful to assess ambulatory patterns?

options.text: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring interpreted using pediatric norms and a standardized approach.
A single home measurement as a substitute for diagnostic confirmation.
Electrocardiography as the blood-pressure confirmation test.
A random urine sodium measurement.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAP guideline recommends ABPM in specified persistent elevated/stage 1 contexts and high-risk situations; home BP can be an adjunct but not a diagnostic replacement. Check current updates and local standards.

practiceQuestions.stem: A term newborn has a creatinine value soon after birth. Which principle should guide interpretation?

options.text: Interpret in the context of postnatal age, maternal/perinatal context and serial trajectory because neonatal renal function is developmentally changing.
Apply an adult reference range without adjustment.
Assume the value is the newborn’s steady-state baseline.
Diagnose congenital CKD from one value.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Neonatal kidney physiology and early postnatal creatinine trajectory require developmental context; a single result does not establish chronic disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: An ultrasound report describes urinary tract dilation in an otherwise stable infant. What is the most appropriate educational interpretation?

options.text: The finding requires interpretation with anatomy, severity, laterality, bladder context, clinical course and appropriate follow-up; dilation alone does not prove functional obstruction.
All dilation proves irreversible renal failure.
Imaging findings replace clinical history and renal function assessment.
The report establishes vesicoureteral reflux.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Structural imaging must be interpreted in context; hydronephrosis/dilation is not equivalent to proven obstruction or reflux.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with CKD has poor linear growth, anemia and abnormal mineral indices. Which conceptual approach best aligns with the ABP blueprint?

options.text: Treat these as potentially connected CKD complications requiring multidomain assessment, not as isolated findings.
Assume anemia alone explains every finding.
Exclude CKD progression because growth is nonspecific.
Use one laboratory value to diagnose all CKD complications.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The pediatric nephrology blueprint explicitly includes CKD progression, mineral/bone disorder, anemia, growth/nutrition and systemic effects as interconnected domains.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child receiving maintenance dialysis reports new symptoms and a change in treatment tolerance. Which course-level learning response is best?

options.text: Consider modality-specific complications, access/circuit or peritoneal factors, adequacy/context and urgent clinical assessment by the responsible team.
Change the prescription independently based on the vignette.
Assume all symptoms are expected and ignore them.
Conclude that transplantation is immediately required.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint includes access, prescription/adequacy and complications in both maintenance HD and PD; real management belongs to the supervising clinical team.

practiceQuestions.stem: A transplanted child has a new rise in creatinine. Which response best reflects board-level differential reasoning?

options.text: Construct a broad allograft dysfunction differential and seek discriminating clinical, laboratory, medication, imaging and transplant-team data.
Diagnose rejection from creatinine alone.
Assume recurrent native disease in every case.
Stop immunosuppression without consultation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Allograft dysfunction has multiple potential causes including rejection, infection, obstruction, medication effects and recurrent/de novo disease; one measurement does not identify the cause.

practiceQuestions.stem: A journal-club learner reads the ABP nephrology content outline. Which statement about its role is most accurate?

options.text: It maps examination domains and approximate weights but is not a complete clinical curriculum or validated study guide.
It proves that completion of this course confers eligibility for certification.
It replaces the ACGME fellowship requirements.
It provides protected official board questions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP explains the outline describes exam content and is not intended as a curriculum or study guide; certification eligibility depends on the board’s current criteria, including accredited training.

title: Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Clinical Fellowship
prerequisites: Physician advanced training; not suitable as substitute residency/fellowship.
Official program describes completed residency in general pediatrics and completed fellowship in pediatric hematology/oncology as prior training.
Program page states board-certified or board-eligible in pediatric hematology/oncology and board-certified in general pediatrics; candidates must verify current application rules directly.
Program described July 1–June 30 for one year; exact annual application deadlines may change.
This independent online course does not confer clinical access, patient responsibilities, faculty supervision, board status or the procedural/clinical competence of the official fellowship.
objectives: Use an age-, site- and symptom-aware framework to organize a pediatric CNS-tumour differential, while identifying urgent supervised review needs and uncertainty.
Interpret molecular/histologic diagnosis through current WHO CNS5 terminology and multidisciplinary evidence review.
Compare major pediatric CNS tumour families and distinguish disease-level evidence, standard approaches, emerging studies and unknowns.
Appraise imaging response, trial design/eligibility and toxicity with pediatric-specific evidence and current source dates.
Integrate family/team communication, neurodevelopment, supportive care and exposure-based survivorship questions.
Map high-level learning goals to the posted ABP PHO Solid Tumors/Brain Tumors and UCNS pediatric CNS outline domains without claiming board equivalence.

objectives: Distinguish supervised advanced clinical fellowship from self-study and describe the named fellowship’s physician prerequisite path.

Differentiate ABP Pediatric Hematology-Oncology certification from broad UCNS Neuro-Oncology certification and the absence of a separate ABP pediatric neuro-oncology certificate.
topics: Childhood/adolescent neurodevelopment, age and tumour-location relevance; scope, family-centred communication, clinical safety and referral/escalation boundaries.
Primary ABP PHO certificate requirements and separate UCNS Neuro-Oncology test/eligibility pathway.
boardDomains: ABP Domain 7: General Oncology Issues; ABP Domain 9: Solid Tumors.
UCNS IV: Systemic Cancer-Related Neurologic Disorders; credential/professional-scope orientation, not an exam subdomain.
units.casePractice: Use a fictional referral note and sort statements into known facts, urgent supervisor escalation cues, missing information and questions requiring the clinical service. No clinical orders or patient-specific advice.
units.assessment: Scope-and-board-map quiz (10 items) plus one source-annotated boundary reflection; all claims cite the relevant board or institutional page.

units.title: Presentations, localization, differential diagnosis and imaging-workup reasoning
objectives: Organize a pediatric CNS-tumour differential around age, location, tempo, neurologic context and associated syndromes without calling any isolated symptom or sign diagnostic.
Explain how clinical examination, imaging, pathology and age/site evidence contribute different roles to diagnosis.
Identify the limits of routine imaging and the need for multidisciplinary review.
topics: Age/site/tempo reasoning; posterior fossa, suprasellar, hemispheric, midline, ventricular and spinal presentations; hydrocephalus and tumour-related neurologic complications.
MRI/neuraxis imaging concepts, modality limitations, pre/postoperative context, neuroradiology and pathology coordination; differential not pattern-matching alone.
boardDomains: ABP Domain 9.F: Solid Tumors—Brain Tumors; Universal Tasks 2 (risk), 3 (diagnosis).
UCNS II.A: Pediatric Primary Nervous System Tumors—Diagnostic Methods.
UCNS IV: increased intracranial pressure, seizures, headache (complication-awareness only).
units.casePractice: Construct a fictional, no-image location/age/tempo vignette; list at least four competing disease families, evidence needed to discriminate and what should be reviewed by neurosurgery, neuroradiology and neuro-oncology.
units.assessment: Structured differential worksheet graded for problem representation, differential breadth, no overclaiming and correctly matched diagnostic roles.

units.title: WHO CNS5 classification, molecular pathology and integrated diagnosis
objectives: Describe why paediatric-type CNS neoplasms require integrated histological, immunohistochemical and molecular classification.
Use a layered pathology-report reading framework that flags missing/discordant molecular data for expert discussion.
Recognize relevant predisposition syndromes and the distinction between germline assessment and tumour profiling.
topics: WHO CNS5 paediatric-type diffuse low-/high-grade gliomas; circumscribed gliomas; ependymomas by site/molecular family; embryonal, glioneuronal, pineal, germ-cell and sellar tumours.
Histology, IHC, sequencing and methylation profiling; integrated diagnosis; inherited cancer predisposition and family referral under clinician/genetics oversight.
boardDomains: ABP Domain 9: Solid Tumors—Brain Tumors; Universal Task 1 (basic science/pathophysiology), 3 (diagnosis).
UCNS II.A: Pediatric Primary Nervous System Tumors—Neuropathologic and laboratory methods.
units.casePractice: Given a fictional report with contradictory morphology and a provisional molecular result, propose a structured list of questions for the neuropathology/molecular tumour board. Do not infer a diagnosis from a single marker.
units.assessment: Integrated-diagnosis table: morphology, site, molecular feature, uncertainty, syndrome question, source/date and expert needed.

units.title: Circumscribed and diffuse low-grade gliomas; glioneuronal tumours
objectives: Compare major paediatric low-grade glioma/glioneuronal families by site, clinical presentation and molecular drivers using current WHO/NCI taxonomy.

UCNS II.A and II.B: pediatric CNS diagnostic methods and therapies.
units.casePractice: Fictional optic-pathway mass: build a differential and evidence ledger covering age/site, vision/function questions, syndrome/genetic evaluation, pathology/molecular confirmation, longitudinal measures and team-based options.
units.assessment: One-page disease evidence matrix with explicit separation of standard, label-supported, off-label and investigational evidence; do not recommend treatment.

mapping.name: Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Clinical Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: One jointly described one-year clinical physician advanced-training offering shared with Boston Children’s Hospital (not a separate second program). Official DFCI/BCH page says the trainee works under pediatric neuro-oncology staff for inpatient/outpatient diagnosis, treatment and long-term follow-up; training areas include neurology, neurosurgery, neuropathology, neuroradiology, nuclear medicine, radiation oncology and neuropsychology; trainee completes a clinical research project, gains Phase I/II trial experience and teaches/supervises PGY-1 General Pediatric Heme-Onc fellows. Schedule July 1–June 30; prerequisites: completed ACGME-accredited general-pediatrics residency and Pediatric Heme-Onc fellowship, general pediatrics board certification, and Pediatric Heme-Onc board certified/eligible. Program-reported centre numbers on the accessed page: >2,000 outpatient visits/year, average 125 new patients/year, >900 survivors followed; institutional self-reports, not independently audited and not a fellow case-volume requirement. unitMap.text: Professional identity, prerequisites, developmental context and safe boundaries
coveredTopics: Childhood/adolescent neurodevelopment, age and tumour-location relevance; scope, family-centred communication, clinical safety and referral/escalation boundaries.
Primary ABP PHO certificate requirements and separate UCNS Neuro-Oncology test/eligibility pathway.

unitMap.text: Presentations, localization, differential diagnosis and imaging-workup reasoning
coveredTopics: Age/site/tempo reasoning; posterior fossa, suprasellar, hemispheric, midline, ventricular and spinal presentations; hydrocephalus and tumour-related neurologic complications.
MRI/neuraxis imaging concepts, modality limitations, pre/postoperative context, neuroradiology and pathology coordination; differential not pattern-matching alone.

unitMap.text: WHO CNS5 classification, molecular pathology and integrated diagnosis
coveredTopics: WHO CNS5 paediatric-type diffuse low-/high-grade gliomas; circumscribed gliomas; ependymomas by site/molecular family; embryonal, glioneuronal, pineal, germ-cell and sellar tumours.
Histology, IHC, sequencing and methylation profiling; integrated diagnosis; inherited cancer predisposition and family referral under clinician/genetics oversight.

unitMap.text: Circumscribed and diffuse low-grade gliomas; glioneuronal tumours
coveredTopics: Pilocytic/circumscribed astrocytic, MAPK-altered diffuse low-grade glioma, optic-pathway tumours, SEGA, PLNTY, DNET, ganglioglioma, diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumour and related rarities.
NF1/TSC and other predisposition context; symptom burden, function, visual/endocrine issues; trial versus approved-label evidence; relapse and surveillance questions.

unitMap.text: Paediatric high-grade glioma and diffuse midline glioma
coveredTopics: H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma; H3 G34-mutant diffuse hemispheric glioma; H3-wildtype/IDH-wildtype paediatric diffuse high-grade glioma; infant-type hemispheric glioma.
Diagnostic integration, clinical trial outcomes/endpoints, pseudoprogression/response limitations, neurologic complications, communication and palliative/supportive domains.

unitMap.text: Medulloblastoma and other CNS embryonal tumours
coveredTopics: Histology, CNS WHO classification, molecular subgroups, dissemination, baseline/staging evaluation, measurable response and relapse.
Treatment-modality concepts and late-effect tradeoffs at a high level; trial enrollment, equipoise and evidence ranking.

unitMap.text: Ependymoma: anatomical and molecular families, response and recurrence
coveredTopics: Supratentorial ZFTA-/YAP1-related entities; posterior-fossa PFA/PFB; spinal categories; myxopapillary ependymoma and site/age context.
Surgical, radiation, recurrence and response concepts; quality/limitations of serial imaging and central review.

unitMap.text: CNS germ-cell, pineal, sellar and craniopharyngioma presentations
coveredTopics: Germinoma and nongerminomatous CNS germ cell tumours; pineal region and embryonal differentials; adamantinomatous and papillary craniopharyngioma.
Diagnosis, staging, endocrine/visual/neurologic sequelae, recurrence, treatment burden and multidisciplinary coordination.

unitMap.text: Spinal and leptomeningeal disease, rare entities and cancer predisposition
coveredTopics: Spinal glioma/ependymoma, leptomeningeal spread, rare/provisional entities, histiocytic mimics as broad differential, inherited predisposition and surveillance.
Rare-disease evidence, central review, pathology review, registry/sample dataset ethics and the role of multicentre trials.

unitMap.text: Multimodal therapy, treatment complications and supportive neuro-oncology
coveredTopics: Surgery and operative pathology interfaces; conventional/proton radiotherapy concepts; cytotoxic, molecularly targeted and immune approaches; clinical-trial contexts.
Seizures, intracranial-pressure symptoms, neurologic deficits, fatigue, endocrine/vision/hearing/cognition, school/family support, palliative care and communication.

unitMap.text: Clinical-trial literacy, response criteria, recurrence and research methods
coveredTopics: NCI/COG/PNOC trial searches; trial status and eligibility disclaimers; phase I–III principles; registries; consent/assent, data sharing and conflict disclosures.
RAPNO and disease-specific response; measurable vs nonmeasurable lesions; pseudoprogression and clinical correlation; recurrence evidence and QI.

unitMap.text: Survivorship, late effects, AYA transitions, equity and integrative synthesis
coveredTopics: COG Long-Term Follow-Up Guidelines; neuropsychology; rehabilitation; school reintegration; AYA/fertility/transition; family communication; access/equity.
Quality improvement, evidence updates, case-resource policy and a final study plan.

topicGaps: No publicly accessible formal DFCI/Boston Children’s dedicated fellowship video archive, schedule or rotation-level instructional-hour map was located; institutional public content is not the whole curriculum.
Only 9.375 verified free recording hours of the 36-hour design floor; residual recorded-video gap is 26.625 hours. Planned clips and authored episodes remain scripts only.

No strong freely accessible specialist-level long-form lecture archive verified for systematic pediatric CNS localization/neuroimaging, operative/radiation planning interfaces, and imaging sequence interpretation; no real scan is recreated in authored lessons.

Molecularly integrated classification and detailed WHO CNS5 pathology instruction across rare pediatric entities are incompletely covered by public recordings; a 2024 corrected open-access review and dated NCI PDQ readings support only selected domains.

Major pediatric tumor families beyond high-grade glioma, ETMR and ependymoma remain thinly represented in the recording ledger, especially CNS germ-cell, pineal/sellar/craniopharyngioma, spinal disease, predisposition syndromes and uncommon glioneuronal entities.

Disease-specific current treatment evidence, response assessment, recurrence, trial design/consent, neurologic toxicity, neuropsychology, rehabilitation, family communication and exposure-based survivorship do not have 36 hours of recorded specialist instruction.

The four newly added foundation webinars are relevant mixed-audience recordings rather than specialist fellowship lectures; use them for orientation and team-role context, not procedural/clinical competence.

Board mapping is cognitive crosswalk only: ABP’s posted PHO outline is effective 2019 and places CNS tumors within broader solid tumors; UCNS outline displays a 2018 revision and is broad neuro-oncology, not a pediatric-only certificate. Verify both before board use.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — Pediatric Hematology-Oncology certificate/exam; prior broad subspecialty relevant to the clinical fellowship, not a Pediatric Neuro-Oncology certificate.

United Council for Neurologic Subspecialties (UCNS) — Neuro-Oncology certification examination; a separate broad neuro-oncology certificate with a pediatric CNS tumour category, not a pediatric-only ABMS/ABP board certificate.

boardStatus.namedClinicalFellowship: Dana-Farber/Boston Children’s Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Clinical Fellowship is a real one-year advanced physician clinical track, not the generic research/laboratory category. Official prerequisites include completed general pediatric residency plus pediatric hematology/oncology fellowship; supervised patient care, the page names multidisciplinary training areas and a clinical research/Phase I/II trial component (without a published rotation timetable). It is not a combined residency/fellowship or degree. The named official page is joint across Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Boston Children’s Hospital; they are institutional variants/sites of this single named offering, not two separate programs or additive curricula. Harvard faculty affiliation is not a claim of ownership/accreditation by Harvard Medical School.
boardStatus.boardExamFinding: No standalone Pediatric Neuro-Oncology certificate is listed by ABP. A separate UCNS Neuro-Oncology certification examination DOES exist: 200 MCQs over four hours; its posted outline includes Adult Primary Nervous System Tumours (35%), Pediatric Primary Nervous System Tumours (25%), Nervous-System Metastases (15%), and Systemic Cancer-Related Neurologic Disorders (25%). The displayed content outline revision is 2018; percentage/domain mapping must be rechecked before a future examination.
boardStatus.eligibilityCaveat: UCNS 2025 eligibility recognizes primary board certification including Pediatrics and Pediatric Hematology-Oncology, but also requires current unrestricted licensure and one of its defined pathways (e.g. a UCNS-accredited fellowship or practice track with prescribed experience/additional conditions). The named DFCI/Boston Children’s public page does not claim UCNS accreditation; completing it alone does not guarantee UCNS eligibility, registration, passage, licensure, or competence.
boardStatus.acgmeStatus: Public DFCI/Boston Children’s material describes a clinical one-year advanced track and does not explicitly state this track’s ACGME accreditation status. The 2026 ACGME requirements cited govern the antecedent Pediatric Hematology-Oncology accredited training pathway, not proof that the additional neuro-oncology offering is ACGME accredited or not accredited. Do not transfer a different institution’s statement about its own fellowship accreditation to DFCI/Boston Children’s.
boardStatus.boardPreparation: Curriculum is a mapped self-study scaffold aligned at a high level to the ABP Pediatric Hematology-Oncology posted Solid Tumors/Brain Tumors domain and the UCNS broad outline. The ABP outline linked is effective from 2019 and the UCNS outline is revised 2018. This is not official question-bank content, coaching, endorsement, certification, eligibility determination or exam readiness.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: The named fellowship’s official prerequisites concern physician training and Pediatric Hematology-Oncology/general-pediatrics certification. No separate ABP Pediatric Neuro-Oncology certificate is listed. UCNS offers a distinct broad Neuro-Oncology certification exam and accepts primary-board-certified pediatric hematology-oncology physicians in principle, but requires current unrestricted licensure and one of its detailed UCNS pathways. The fellowship page does not claim UCNS accreditation or automatically establish any candidate’s eligibility. Verify the current primary board, UCNS eligibility policy and application directly; this course confers neither board eligibility nor certification.

officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Clinical Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: One jointly described one-year clinical physician advanced-training offering shared with Boston Children’s Hospital (not a separate second program). Official DFCI/BCH page says the trainee works under pediatric neuro-oncology staff for inpatient/outpatient diagnosis, treatment and long-term follow-up; training areas include neurology, neurosurgery, neuropathology, neuroradiology, nuclear medicine, radiation oncology and neuropsychology; trainee completes a clinical research project, gains Phase I/II trial experience and teaches/supervises PGY-1 General Pediatric Heme-Onc fellows. Schedule July 1–June 30; prerequisites: completed ACGME-accredited general-pediatrics residency and Pediatric Heme-Onc fellowship, general pediatrics board certification, and Pediatric Heme-Onc board certified/eligible. Program-reported centre numbers on the accessed page: >2,000 outpatient visits/year, average 125 new patients/year, >900 survivors followed; institutional self-reports, not independently audited and not a fellow case-volume requirement. No program-specific ACGME or UCNS accreditation assertion was found on the programme page.

officialProgrammes.name: Pediatric Neuro-Oncology Clinical Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The same jointly named clinical advanced fellowship as the Dana-Farber entry; both are Harvard Medical School teaching affiliates. It is one offering, not additive/double-counted. The official page states clinical service, supervised patient care, the multidisciplinary experiences and research components in the DFCI entry. The website does not publish a required lecture/video schedule or accessible dedicated lecture archive.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The DFCI/Boston Children’s primary page confirms a real one-year clinical physician programme, supervised direct care, interdisciplinary training, trial exposure and a clinical research project—not a research-only job or generic directory bucket. It identifies training areas in neurology, neurosurgery, neuropathology, neuroradiology, nuclear medicine, radiation oncology and neuropsychology, but does not publish a date-block rotation schedule or hour-by-area breakdown. The two host names are exact variants of one jointly described programme. The page does not say this offering is a combined residency/fellowship or list it as ACGME/UCNS accredited. The parent Pediatric Heme-Onc page mentions weekly CNS didactics that are mostly recorded/archived, but supplies no public recording links, so it is not misrepresented or counted as this track’s own accessible curriculum. No Johns Hopkins variant is being asserted for this one-assignment deliverable. Institutional volumes above are webpage statements only; no invented case/diagnosis volumes.

topicGaps: No publicly accessible formal DFCI/Boston Children’s dedicated fellowship video archive, schedule or rotation-level instructional-hour map was located; institutional public content is not the whole curriculum.
Only 9.375 verified free recording hours of the 36-hour design floor; residual recorded-video gap is 26.625 hours. Planned clips and authored episodes remain scripts only.

No strong freely accessible specialist-level long-form lecture archive verified for systematic pediatric CNS localization/neuroimaging, operative/radiation planning interfaces, and imaging sequence interpretation; no real scan is recreated in authored lessons.

Molecularly integrated classification and detailed WHO CNS5 pathology instruction across rare pediatric entities are incompletely covered by public recordings; a 2024 corrected open-access review and dated NCI PDQ readings support only selected domains.

Major pediatric tumor families beyond high-grade glioma, ETMR and ependymoma remain thinly represented in the recording ledger, especially CNS germ-cell, pineal/sellar/craniopharyngioma, spinal disease, predisposition syndromes and uncommon glioneuronal entities.

Disease-specific current treatment evidence, response assessment, recurrence, trial design/consent, neurologic toxicity, neuropsychology, rehabilitation, family communication and exposure-based survivorship do not have 36 hours of recorded specialist instruction.

The four newly added foundation webinars are relevant mixed-audience recordings rather than specialist fellowship lectures; use them for orientation and team-role context, not procedural/clinical competence.

Board mapping is cognitive crosswalk only: ABP’s posted PHO outline is effective 2019 and places CNS tumors within broader solid tumors; UCNS outline displays a 2018 revision and is broad neuro-oncology, not a pediatric-only certificate. Verify both before board use.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

It is a research-only degree for nonphysicians.
Its completion guarantees state licensure.

Summarize neurologic critical care priorities and explain prognosis limits.
units.prerequisites: Medical degree-level neuroscience, pediatric history/physical examination, basic neurology, evidence appraisal; this independent course is not clinical skills training.
topics: Raised ICP; optic disc swelling; tumor syndromes; neurocritical care; brain injury; neuroprognostication; palliative care.
units.assessment: Structured review of a public case with proposed multidisciplinary questions. Rubric: localization (25%), urgency (25%), multidisciplinary plan (25%), ethical uncertainty/communication (25%).

assignment.title: Longitudinal case reasoning portfolio
assignment.instructions: For four linked, public Child Neurology Society teaching cases, prepare an independently written history/phenotype summary, localization and differential, test rationale, family-centered communication note, and evidence-based source list. Cases are assigned as links only; do not copy images/text or include personal health information.
assignment.rubric: Each submission is scored 0–4 on chronology/phenotype, localization, prioritized differential, evidence/test rationale, uncertainty/safety, and communication. 3 = clear and well-supported; 2 = partially supported; 1 = major omissions; 0 = absent/unsafe. A pass threshold is a course design suggestion, not clinical validation or board prediction.

topicGaps: Observed accessible unique recording time is 22.4514 hours; the 36-hour video target remains short by 13.5486 hours. Script targets and learner time do not count as rendered/verified media.

Insufficient source-backed recorded instruction remains in pediatric EEG acquisition/interpretation, electroclinical syndrome distinctions, infantile spasms, and an age-specific first-seizure pathway.

Neonatal neurology is improved by one full lecture, but detailed neonatal examination, encephalopathy, neuroimaging, EEG interpretation and metabolic emergency reasoning still need more age-specific instruction.

Pediatric stroke and vascular disease remain weakly covered by lectures; the existing source outline maps topics but requires current local pediatric stroke protocols and supervised clinical experience.

Neurogenetics and treatable metabolic disorders have useful public overviews, but test selection, variant interpretation, metabolic emergencies and family counseling still need deeper, current, disease-specific teaching.
Neuromuscular lecture time improved, but systematic pediatric UMN/LMN/NMJ/muscle localization, respiratory/bulbar assessment and current diagnosis/therapy distinctions remain insufficiently covered.

Neuro-oncology, neuro-ophthalmology, pediatric neurocritical care, sleep/cognition/psychiatric comorbidity, and the 40% adult-neurology blueprint component need deeper mapped teaching; breadth of the unit list exceeds demonstrated recorded coverage.
Public lecture runtimes and release dates are not evidence that recommendations remain current; guideline/source updates and direct clinician teaching remain necessary.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN): Neurology Certification Examination with Special Qualification in Child Neurology (initial certification)
medical.boardStatus: A separate child-neurology initial certification examination exists: ABPN Neurology with Special Qualification in Child Neurology. No separate “pediatric neurology board” under a distinct certifier is claimed here. The exam includes 60% child-neurology and 40% adult-neurology content per the December 15, 2025 ABPN blueprint. ACGME accreditation is program accreditation, not board certification.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This self-study course does not confer ABPN eligibility. ABPN requires qualifying medical degree, approved/accredited training, license and other applicable requirements. Confirm current requirements directly with ABPN.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Children’s Center (Baltimore, Maryland)

officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official listing calls it ACGME Accredited; describes a three-year pediatric neurology residency phase following two years of general pediatrics. The detailed program overview describes PGY-3 to PGY-5 and inpatient/outpatient adult and pediatric neurology, subspecialty, elective, neurophysiology, child psychiatry and neuropathology experiences. officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital (St. Petersburg, Florida)
officialProgrammes.name: Child Neurology Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Separate exact institutional offering, not merged with Baltimore. Its page labels the five-year program ACGME-accredited and describes two years pediatric residency, one year adult neurology at USF/Tampa General and two years child neurology, with Johns Hopkins All Children’s and affiliate rotations.

medical.programmeSourceScope: These are distinct physician child/pediatric neurology clinical residencies at two Johns Hopkins institutions with different curriculum structures. Hopkins Baltimore details are supported by the official program page and full curriculum overview. All Children’s explicitly reports a five-year program and claims ACGME accreditation; the listing is treated as the institution’s public statement, not independently matched against the live ACGME registry. This is neither a generic directory category nor a research-only/non-physician track, nor an explicitly combined dual-specialty residency. ABPN initial child-neurology certification is a qualification on the Neurology certification examination, not a separate board sponsor.
sourceCaveats: No prior MED-165 artifact or saved research was present in either named prior-work location at task start.
Hopkins Baltimore official directory confirms ACGME-accredited physician residency; its details page and directory disagree on residents per year, so inconsistency is preserved.

topicGaps: Observed accessible unique recording time is 22.4514 hours; the 36-hour video target remains short by 13.5486 hours. Script targets and learner time do not count as rendered/verified media.

Insufficient source-backed recorded instruction remains in pediatric EEG acquisition/interpretation, electroclinical syndrome distinctions, infantile spasms, and an age-specific first-seizure pathway.

Neonatal neurology is improved by one full lecture, but detailed neonatal examination, encephalopathy, neuroimaging, EEG interpretation and metabolic emergency reasoning still need more age-specific instruction.

Pediatric stroke and vascular disease remain weakly covered by lectures; the existing source outline maps topics but requires current local pediatric stroke protocols and supervised clinical experience.

Neurogenetics and treatable metabolic disorders have useful public overviews, but test selection, variant interpretation, metabolic emergencies and family counseling still need deeper, current, disease-specific teaching.
Neuromuscular lecture time improved, but systematic pediatric UMN/LMN/NMJ/muscle localization, respiratory/bulbar assessment and current diagnosis/therapy distinctions remain insufficiently covered.

Neuro-oncology, neuro-ophthalmology, pediatric neurocritical care, sleep/cognition/psychiatric comorbidity, and the 40% adult-neurology blueprint component need deeper mapped teaching; breadth of the unit list exceeds demonstrated recorded coverage.
Public lecture runtimes and release dates are not evidence that recommendations remain current; guideline/source updates and direct clinician teaching remain necessary.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has brief, recurrent events with stereotyped unilateral facial clonic activity and speech arrest; awareness appears preserved. What is the best first reasoning step?

options.text: Assume generalized epilepsy from age alone
Clarify event semiology and evaluate focal onset while considering mimics
Diagnose a specific syndrome without EEG or history
Order broad metabolic testing for every event

practiceQuestions.rationale: Semiology, awareness and context guide seizure classification; do not force syndrome diagnosis before sufficient history and indicated testing.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional child continues convulsing at 12 minutes despite initial stabilization. Which statement best matches the AES 2016 framework?

options.text: Delay all treatment until 30 minutes
At 5–20 minutes, a benzodiazepine is recommended as initial therapy in the guideline framework
Use paralytics alone to stop seizures
Third-line anesthetics are always first choice

practiceQuestions.rationale: AES guideline phases emphasize stabilization followed by initial benzodiazepine therapy when intervention is needed; local current pathway governs care.

practiceQuestions.stem: A toddler misses one CDC checklist item. What conclusion is justified?

options.text: The child has a developmental disorder
The checklist is a diagnostic test
The item prompts conversation and may support formal validated screening/evaluation; it is not a diagnosis
No further follow-up is ever needed

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC states checklists are communication tools and not screening/diagnostic instruments; concerns warrant formal screening/evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age patient has recurrent headache with a newly documented swollen optic disc. What is the best cognitive approach?

options.text: Treat as uncomplicated migraine without evaluation
Consider papilledema/raised ICP and secondary causes; urgent evaluation depends on clinical context
Assume pseudopapilledema without examination
Use a normal prior headache history to exclude new pathology

practiceQuestions.rationale: Papilledema requires a secondary cause/raised intracranial pressure differential and appropriate clinical evaluation; headache red flags change workup.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with motor delay has hypertonia and asymmetric hand use. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Classify function and phenotype, assess trajectory/associated impairments, and consider targeted etiologic assessment
Use milestones alone to diagnose cerebral palsy
Wait until school age to evaluate
Assume all hypertonia is spasticity

practiceQuestions.rationale: A developmental/neurologic assessment combines motor phenotype, trajectory and function; milestone checklists do not diagnose.

practiceQuestions.stem: Genetic testing identifies a variant of uncertain significance in a child with seizures. What is the safest interpretation?

options.text: It proves the causal diagnosis
It should be treated as pathogenic without phenotype review
Interpret with phenotype, inheritance, classification limits and genetics expertise; do not equate VUS with diagnosis
Ignore family history

practiceQuestions.rationale: Variant interpretation requires phenotype and classification context; a VUS is not a confirmed molecular diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A febrile child develops acute confusion and focal seizures. Which broad initial framing is best?

options.text: Encephalitis is excluded if fever is modest
Urgently evaluate infectious, inflammatory, metabolic and seizure-related causes in parallel
Assume primary psychiatric illness
Defer assessment until outpatient follow-up

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute encephalopathy with seizures is an emergency; infectious and other treatable etiologies require prompt assessment according to current protocols.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has abrupt focal weakness. Which assumption should be avoided?

options.text: Stroke is in the differential and warrants urgent evaluation
Pediatric causes and pathways differ from adult stroke
Adult diagnostic/treatment algorithms can be applied without age-specific review
Time and neurologic localization matter

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric stroke evaluation and therapeutic decisions require pediatric-specific expertise; adult algorithms should not be imported uncritically.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a child with progressive symmetric weakness, which examination finding most directly helps localization?

options.text: Tone, reflexes, distribution, fatigability, sensory pattern and bulbar/respiratory status together
Family history alone
A single serum biomarker without examination
Age alone

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pattern-based localization precedes targeted tests and urgent respiratory/bulbar safety assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes the ABPN Child Neurology initial certification blueprint as of Dec 2025?

options.text: 100% child-neurology questions
60% child neurology and 40% adult neurology questions
Board eligibility arises from completion of this course
ACGME accreditation and ABPN exam blueprint are the same thing

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN specifies 60% child and 40% adult neurology exam questions; training and certification eligibility have separate requirements.

assumedKnowledge: Neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and child development basics
Adult neurological-surgery training concepts and medical literature appraisal
Basic neuroradiology terminology; no diagnostic authority inferred
notProvided: No admissions eligibility determination, supervised clinical training, cases/procedures, patient data, credential, license or board eligibility.

objectives: Synthesize age-dependent developmental anatomy, history/examination and pediatric imaging questions.
