Practice original board-style cognition without reproducing protected examination items or predicting board success.
Recognize licensing, rights, privacy and credential limits for videos, cases, datasets, and institutional program claims.

units.title: Developmental neuroanatomy, examination, and pediatric imaging reasoning
objectives: Relate age-dependent neurodevelopment and skull/spinal anatomy to presentation without overgeneralizing adult patterns.
Construct a problem representation and localize findings while keeping urgent deterioration distinct from elective assessment.
Select imaging questions and recognize modality limits; explain when expert pediatric neuroradiology input is needed.
topics: Neurodevelopment and age-adjusted neurologic examination
Cranial sutures, CSF spaces, posterior fossa and spinal dysraphism anatomy
CT/MRI/ultrasound and radiation-conscious imaging questions
Image interpretation as a team-based cognitive skill
boardDomains: Clinical assessment and neuroimaging; educator-created crosswalk, not an official exam blueprint
units.casePractice: Use the freely accessible, de-identified TCIA BraTS-PEDs MRI dataset only under its stated terms; make a written modality/sequence observation, not a diagnosis or treatment plan.
units.assessment: Short-answer localization exercise scored for age context (25%), anatomy/localization (35%), imaging limits (25%), uncertainty/safety statement (15%).

units.title: CSF physiology, hydrocephalus, shunts, and endoscopic third ventriculostomy
objectives: Explain communicating and noncommunicating mechanisms and differential etiologies of childhood hydrocephalus.
Compare CSF diversion options conceptually using anatomy, age, etiology, and evidence, not a single universal algorithm.
Recognize that shunt/ETV failure and infection require urgent clinician-led assessment; evaluate guideline evidence quality.
topics: Congenital/acquired hydrocephalus
Ventricular anatomy, ETV, ETV/CPC, shunt failure and infection
Neonatal IVH-associated hydrocephalus and tumors
Outcome metrics and evidence uncertainty
units.casePractice: Read linked section lecture and CNS guideline text; no private case record or image is supplied.
units.assessment: Evidence grid: clinical question, recommendation strength/date, comparator, outcome, limitation; 20-point rubric: accuracy 40%, evidence grading 30%, uncertainty 20%, citation 10%.

units.title: Craniosynostosis and craniofacial collaboration
objectives: Distinguish suture fusion from positional head-shape variation using history, examination, growth and appropriate imaging concepts.

Compare endoscopic/helmet and open vault-remodeling concepts as context-dependent options without procedural instruction.
topics: Sagittal, metopic, coronal, lambdoid and multisuture patterns
Syndromic assessment, intracranial pressure surveillance, imaging tradeoffs
Timing, team care, shared decisions, outcomes and guideline jurisdiction

units.title: Neural-tube defects, dysraphism, Chiari, tethering, and fetal repair
objectives: Differentiate open myelomeningocele from selected closed dysraphism concepts and identify the need for multidisciplinary follow-up.

Prenatal repair evidence and maternal/fetal tradeoffs
Hydrocephalus, Chiari II, tethered cord and long-term surveillance
Chiari I complexity and symptom/imaging correlation

units.assessment: One-page recommendation matrix scored evidence correctness 45%, population/qualification 25%, surveillance caveat 20%, source accuracy 10%.

units.title: Pediatric brain and spinal tumors: localization, imaging and modern classification
objectives: Develop a differential that accounts for age, compartment, location, dissemination and hydrocephalus.
Interpret the limits of imaging-only inference and explain why histologic/molecular classification matters.
Use current NCI PDQ index to trace tumor-specific management summaries and flag update dates.
topics: Supratentorial/infratentorial, ventricular and pineal lesions
Embryonal, glial, ependymal, germ-cell, choroid-plexus and sellar-region tumors
Hydrocephalus, tissue diagnosis, molecular era and multidisciplinary neuro-oncology

units.assessment: Structured differential matrix; score age/location (30%), differential (30%), image limits (20%), tissue/molecular caveat (10%), citations (10%).

units.title: Tumor surgery reasoning, treatment interfaces, and outcomes
objectives: Frame resectability and functional/anatomic risk at a conceptual level with multidisciplinary input.
Distinguish educational review of treatment pathways from individualized oncology decisions.
Identify evidence gaps, terminology changes, and source dates when reading pediatric tumor literature.
topics: Preoperative goals and tradeoffs
Choroid plexus tumors, pineal-region and supratentorial lesions
Hydrocephalus, tissue diagnosis, adjuvant therapy interfaces
Functional outcomes, surveillance and family communication
units.casePractice: Use NCI PDQ public evidence summaries and TCIA BraTS-PEDs where appropriate; no uploaded images.
units.assessment: Multidisciplinary tumor-board memo using a fictional vignette; rubric: issue framing 25%, options/evidence 35%, uncertainty 20%, family-centered language 10%, citations 10%.

units.title: Pediatric epilepsy surgery evaluation and procedures
objectives: Describe referral after drug-resistant epilepsy assessment and the role of a multidisciplinary epilepsy conference.

Compare resection, disconnection, ablation and neuromodulation at a high level and distinguish seizure-freedom from palliation goals.

Focal lesions, hemispheric disease, callosotomy/hemispherotomy and stereo-EEG
Outcome classification, cognition, family goals and safety

units.assessment: Conference synthesis exercise scored concordance analysis 35%, alternatives 25%, outcome goals 20%, limitations/citations 20%.

units.title: Pediatric cerebrovascular lesions
objectives: Classify broad pediatric vascular neurosurgical problems and distinguish vascular malformations from other lesions.

Use open lectures as topic introductions and return to up-to-date institution-specific clinical guidance.
topics: AVMs and hemorrhagic presentation concepts
Imaging and multidisciplinary neurovascular review
Cerebral vascular development and selection limits
units.casePractice: View the public section AVM talk (YouTube); no patient image reproduction or treatment instruction.
units.assessment: One-page differential/decision-map exercise, scored anatomy 30%, evidence and uncertainty 30%, team/safety 20%, references 20%.

units.title: Pediatric neurotrauma, craniocervical injury, and safeguarding
objectives: Use a structured injury history/examination and distinguish mild TBI guidance from urgent neurosurgical trauma.
Apply CDC mTBI guidance to avoid routine imaging for uncomplicated mTBI while recognizing it is not a severe-injury protocol.
Discuss safeguarding/non-accidental trauma with a multidisciplinary, non-stereotyping, evidence-based approach.

Pediatric cervical/craniocervical differences and instability concepts
CDC mTBI assessment, imaging, recovery and return to activity
Safeguarding and documentation as clinician responsibilities

units.assessment: Guideline applicability note; rubric scope 35%, risk distinctions 25%, appropriate source 25%, safe wording 15%.

units.title: Functional, movement, spasticity, and peripheral nerve topics
objectives: Explain the multidisciplinary context of pediatric spasticity, cerebral palsy and selective dorsal rhizotomy (SDR).

Describe a pediatric peripheral nerve/brachial plexus workup at a conceptual level without procedural competence claims.

Movement disorders
Pediatric brachial plexus assessment and intervention concepts
Function, participation and patient-reported outcomes
units.casePractice: Linked public videos are original publisher content; no cases/images may be extracted or reused without rights.
units.assessment: Multidisciplinary goal map, scored patient/family goals 30%, roles 30%, evidence/limits 25%, citations 15%.

units.title: Perioperative, critical care, complications, communication, and ethics
objectives: Identify key perioperative collaboration domains relevant to complex pediatric neurosurgical care.
Use escalation/complication recognition as a learning objective, not a substitute for emergency protocols.

Postoperative surveillance, infection and device complications
Consent/assent, communication, ethics and quality improvement

units.assessment: Structured handoff simulation using a fictional case; rubric critical facts 35%, uncertainty/escalation 25%, concise communication 20%, family context 10%, safety boundaries 10%.

units.title: Research literacy, outcomes, coding, and exam-style clinical reasoning
objectives: Read guideline recommendation strength, population, outcome and evidence limits.
Interpret outcome measures and avoid treating case volume or a brief exam as competence.
Use original questions to practice reasoning, recognizing that no official ABPNS detailed blueprint was publicly located.
topics: Study design and evidence appraisal
Q/I, registries, outcome measures and case-log boundaries
Pediatric neurosurgery coding lecture (supplementary; coding is not a clinical board blueprint)
Clinical reasoning and question critique
boardDomains: Supplementary administrative coding; board mapping not claimed
units.casePractice: No cases copied. Use published datasets only under their own terms; citations required.
units.assessment: Question-writing exercise and evidence critique; accuracy 40%, rationale 25%, source 20%, scope/qualification 15%.

assignment.title: Evidence-aware topic dossier
assignment.instructions: Select one unit. Write a two-page dossier with the clinical question, age/population, differential or options, an authoritative source statement, evidence strength/date, what is unknown, and a multidisciplinary referral/communication map. Use no real patient details.
assignment.passThreshold: 70/100 for self-study only; not validated competency.

assignment.title: Original board-style question set and critique
assignment.instructions: Write two original questions for a course objective, identify one best answer, explain all distractors, cite the source, and tag the cognitive task (recall, interpretation, prioritization, evidence evaluation). Do not reproduce board items or claim predictive validity.
assignment.passThreshold: 80/100 for completion; not a board-passing predictor.

assignment.title: Multidisciplinary conference synthesis (fictional prompt)
assignment.instructions: Use a provided fictional prompt with incomplete data. State missing information, competing interpretations, evidence needed, team roles, safety escalation triggers and why no treatment recommendation can be made from incomplete context.

assessment.format: Formative self-study: 10 original multiple-choice questions, three rubric-scored assignments, and unit retrieval prompts. Suggested completion standard is 80% on the question set and assignment rubrics; no exam validity or board prediction is established.
assessment.feedback: Self-check against cited source and rubric; errors in current clinical guidance require human specialist review before clinical use.
assessment.limitations: No psychometric validation, human clinical review, examination blueprint, or predictive validity.

studyHours.plan: Suggested self-study plan, not recorded-video time: 12 units × 4 hours = 48 hours reading, note-making, question practice and assignments, plus 22.18 verified specialty video hours and 1.19 supplemental coding video hours, for approximately 71.37 planned learner-hours if all current videos are watched. This is a study plan only, not training credit. Original planned clips are excluded.

topicGaps: No publicly fetched formal ABPNS examination content outline or detailed domain weightings; the board/domain crosswalk remains educator-created. The existence of pathway-specific pediatric focused-practice written/oral assessment does not make this fellowship an independent board or confer eligibility.

The 36-hour specialty-video runtime floor is met by distinct observed specialty recordings; the 1.1922 supplementary coding hours are outside that specialty count. No complete public Hopkins didactic syllabus, rotation schedule, institutional cases, proprietary teaching catalog or clinical training hours are available in the public sources reviewed.

The 22 added ISPN videos are public archive recordings, many are debate-format and/or topic snapshots from older series. They are useful for contrasting reasoning, not authority for current recommendations; check each topic against current authoritative sources. Current ISPN Library material advertised as member-library content is not included.

Source-backed video/lecture coverage remains comparatively sparse for pediatric CNS infection outside postinfectious hydrocephalus, spinal tumors, comprehensive cerebrovascular malformations, neurocritical care protocols, longitudinal neurodevelopmental outcomes and rare syndromic disorders. Readings and scripted episodes introduce, but do not close, these specialty-content gaps.
Several AANS/CNS archive items linked through Google Drive still have unknown direct access/runtime and remain explicitly uncounted. No estimates were assigned.

The added items were publicly listed with direct watch URLs on the official ISPN channel. Individual watch-player playback was not replay-tested for every item after YouTube rate-limited repeated metadata requests; recheck availability at course release.

Some CNS guidelines are older evidence reviews (the myelomeningocele search covered through September 2016); recheck guideline status, newer evidence and jurisdiction before any clinical interpretation.
Human clinical review was not performed; no clinical competence, care authorization, licensure, fellowship eligibility, board eligibility or exam-readiness claim is made.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship; post-neurological-surgery residency; ACPNF-accredited/non-ACGME standalone pediatric fellowship
boardNames: American Board of Pediatric Neurological Surgery (ABPNS)
ABMS-recognized Focused Practice Designation in Pediatric Neurological Surgery (administered by ABNS/ABPNS)
medical.boardStatus: The Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital variants appear as Accredited in the independent ACPNF program directory (as-of dates 2026-01-02 and 2026-01-22 respectively). ACPNF is not ACGME. ABPNS states that the current North American process yields a pediatric neurosurgery subspecialty credential/focused-practice designation and includes a pediatric written focused-practice examination, qualifying practice case log, and pediatric focused oral examination (pathway-specific). This is not automatic upon fellowship completion and is distinct from primary ABNS certification. ABMS approves the RFPD; ABNS and ABPNS manage it.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course confers no eligibility. Current ABPNS pathway requirements vary with ABNS or Royal College certification, ACPNF-accredited fellowship timing, licensure/privileges, practice case logs and examinations. ABNS primary certification has separate requirements including ACGME-accredited neurological-surgery residency and current written/case-log/oral/tracking rules. Verify current rules directly with ABNS, ABPNS, ACPNF and applicable licensing bodies. No promised pass or qualification.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet’s initial single Baltimore listing is expanded only to preserve the separately verified Johns Hopkins All Children’s clinical variant. ACPNF publicly lists Johns Hopkins Hospital (Baltimore; Johns Hopkins University affiliation) and Johns Hopkins All Children’s Hospital (St. Petersburg; Johns Hopkins University affiliation) as separate accredited programs with distinct sites and directors. Their exact official names and campuses are retained. The School of Medicine directory labels the Baltimore listing “Non-Standard”; the ACPNF directory separately lists it Accredited. All Children’s says ACPNF-certified. ACPNF is an independent fellowship accreditor; current ACGME Neurological Surgery requirements page lists neurological surgery residency and neurocritical care/neuroendovascular intervention, not pediatric neurosurgery fellowship as a standalone ACGME subspecialty. Institution pages do not publish a complete proprietary didactic curriculum.
sourceCaveats: ACPNF profile dates are taken as shown on the directory page, not a live institutional accreditation certification.
Hopkins has two distinct official-campus variants. Directory and program pages use different shorthand; exact source wording is preserved in programme notes.
ACGME accredits neurological-surgery residency; ACPNF independently accredits pediatric neurosurgery fellowship. Avoid calling either a fellowship “ACGME pediatric neurosurgery accreditation.”
ABPNS process page revised 2026-04-19. Requirements may change; applicants must consult official boards. No detailed exam blueprint was found.
Public lecture channel runtime labels were observed 2026-10-07; the publisher may change/remove videos. Runtime/access should be rechecked at each course release.
No individual hospital rotations, case volumes, eligibility guarantees, institutional proprietary lecture catalog, or outcome claims were inferred.
Human clinical review is not performed. Curriculum is not affiliated with Johns Hopkins, ABNS, ABPNS, ABMS, ACGME, AANS/CNS, or ACPNF.

The 36-hour specialty-video runtime floor is met by distinct observed specialty recordings; the 1.1922 supplementary coding hours are outside that specialty count. No complete public Hopkins didactic syllabus, rotation schedule, institutional cases, proprietary teaching catalog or clinical training hours are available in the public sources reviewed.

The 22 added ISPN videos are public archive recordings, many are debate-format and/or topic snapshots from older series. They are useful for contrasting reasoning, not authority for current recommendations; check each topic against current authoritative sources. Current ISPN Library material advertised as member-library content is not included.

Source-backed video/lecture coverage remains comparatively sparse for pediatric CNS infection outside postinfectious hydrocephalus, spinal tumors, comprehensive cerebrovascular malformations, neurocritical care protocols, longitudinal neurodevelopmental outcomes and rare syndromic disorders. Readings and scripted episodes introduce, but do not close, these specialty-content gaps.
Several AANS/CNS archive items linked through Google Drive still have unknown direct access/runtime and remain explicitly uncounted. No estimates were assigned.

The added items were publicly listed with direct watch URLs on the official ISPN channel. Individual watch-player playback was not replay-tested for every item after YouTube rate-limited repeated metadata requests; recheck availability at course release.

Some CNS guidelines are older evidence reviews (the myelomeningocele search covered through September 2016); recheck guideline status, newer evidence and jurisdiction before any clinical interpretation.
Human clinical review was not performed; no clinical competence, care authorization, licensure, fellowship eligibility, board eligibility or exam-readiness claim is made.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public educational module asks what makes pediatric craniosynostosis assessment more than a cosmetic inspection. Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Use head shape alone to assign a diagnosis and operation.
Integrate age, history, growth, examination, syndrome features, and imaging only as indicated with a multidisciplinary team.
Obtain CT in every child before any examination.
Use adult cranial-growth assumptions without adjustment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Guideline-based assessment includes recognition/referral and multidisciplinary expertise; diagnosis and management are not reducible to a single shape or scan. The linked open version is a Dutch patient/family version, not an American clinical protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best represents the CNS myelomeningocele guideline’s qualified evidence statement on prenatal closure?

options.text: It is recommended for every fetus with myelomeningocele without eligibility constraints.
For fetuses meeting maternal/fetal MOMS criteria, prenatal closure is recommended to reduce shunt-dependent hydrocephalus risk; tradeoffs and individual factors remain relevant.
It guarantees normal long-term ambulation.
It eliminates need for tethered-cord surveillance.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline explicitly conditions the recommendation on meeting maternal and fetal MOMS criteria, identifies short-term ambulatory benefit with uncertainty about long-term benefit, and recommends ongoing surveillance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner compares pediatric hydrocephalus strategies. What is the appropriate use of the CNS guideline?

options.text: Treat it as a fixed protocol for every patient.
Treat it as an evidence-based educational aid whose recommendations require attention to population, question, and clinical context.
Assume one CSF diversion strategy is universally best.
Ignore complications because the guideline focuses on procedures.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CNS guideline states it is an educational tool, not a fixed protocol, and evaluates interventions, complications, and evidence gaps.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement matches current CDC pediatric mild-TBI guidance?

options.text: Routinely image every child to establish mTBI.
Do not routinely image to diagnose mTBI; use validated age-appropriate symptom scales and provide gradual return guidance.
Require complete inactivity for at least two weeks.
Use adult scales for all children.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CDC page updated 2025-07-29 explicitly states no routine imaging for diagnosis, validated age-appropriate symptom scales, and gradual return to non-sports activity after no more than 1–2 days of rest. This applies to mTBI, not a rule for severe injury.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why should a pediatric CNS tumor differential use histology and molecular classification in addition to location?

options.text: Location alone determines modern tumor identity.
Tumor location/extent and histologic plus molecular findings contribute distinct information to classification and management context.
Molecular findings are irrelevant in children.
Imaging proves histologic subtype.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ describes tumor classification as histologic with location/extent important, and immunohistochemical/cytogenetic/molecular findings increasingly used.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pediatric brain-tumor imaging collection is used for a teaching exercise. Which rights practice is correct for TCIA BraTS-PEDs?

options.text: Re-identify images because they are public.
Cite the dataset DOI, honor CC BY 4.0 attribution, do not identify/contact participants, and do not rehost without satisfying applicable repository requirements.
Assume all images are public domain.
Remove the source citation when adapting an image.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The collection lists CC BY 4.0 and data-citation requirements; TCIA policies prohibit attempts to identify/contact participants and impose citation/attribution and mirroring conditions.

practiceQuestions.stem: In current ABPNS/ABNS materials, what is the accurate characterization of the pediatric neurosurgery credential pathway?

options.text: A fellowship alone automatically grants primary ABNS certification.

The current framework describes a pediatric focused-practice subspecialty credential involving a written exam, eligible pathway/case log, and pediatric oral examination; primary ABNS certification has separate requirements.
There is no pediatric focused exam.
ACGME accredits all pediatric neurosurgery fellowships.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPNS states its current process gives a subspecialty credential and lists written, case-log and oral components; ABNS training rules separately concern primary certification; ACPNF is an independent fellowship accreditor.

practiceQuestions.stem: A case-discussion recording contains real clinical imaging and is freely viewable online. What may the independent course safely assume?

options.text: Free viewing grants ownership and rehosting rights.
It may link learners to the publisher-hosted video but must not copy or republish images absent permission or a compatible license.
De-identification automatically makes every image public domain.
A lecture recording can be sold if the original is free.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The section archive links publicly hosted teaching, but its page does not provide a broad image-reuse license. Free-to-view is not a license to republish clinical imagery.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which reasoning statement is appropriate when epilepsy presurgical information is discordant?

options.text: One test always overrides all other evidence.
Integrate semiology, EEG, imaging and functional/neuropsychological information in a multidisciplinary hypothesis-driven review, and state uncertainty.
Proceed directly to surgery based on one seizure description.
A lecture alone establishes candidacy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The section’s public epilepsy lecture describes multimodal presurgical evaluation and multidisciplinary conference; this course teaches synthesis, not candidacy decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct interpretation of the 36-hour curriculum floor and the open lecture archive?

options.text: Planned scripts may be counted now as recorded hours.
Only distinct, publicly accessible recordings with observed runtimes count; planned clips remain plans until produced and verified.
A duplicated talk counts twice if it covers two modules.
An unverified drive link can be assigned an estimated duration.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The contract explicitly requires real unique video IDs, observed durations and free-access status; plans, estimates, duplicates, and unknown runtimes are not ready hours.

title: Pediatric Ophthalmology and Adult Strabismus Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Postgraduate physician self-study for learners who have completed foundational ophthalmic/medical training; not a clinical credentialing pathway. Suitable as advanced theory for ophthalmology residents/fellows and clinicians reviewing pediatric eye/strabismus topics.
assumedKnowledge: Basic ocular anatomy, optics, refraction and examination
General medical reasoning and pediatric development
Ability to read clinical guidelines and distinguish evidence from expert judgement
prerequisites.sequence: Complete Units 1–12 in order; revisit the relevant linked cases and sources. Skills videos in Unit 6/7 are observational only.

objectives: Structure a careful age-appropriate pediatric ophthalmic examination and separate screening from diagnosis.
Reason across amblyopia, strabismus, pediatric anterior segment, retina, neuro-ophthalmology, genetics and urgent presentations.
Interpret ocular alignment, age-appropriate visual function, history and cycloplegic refraction in context.
Recognize red flags and appropriate urgency without diagnosing from an isolated sign or image.
Use current authoritative sources and explain uncertainty, evidence limits, ethics and licensing.
Distinguish general U.S. ophthalmology board certification from the separate European FEBOS-SP subspecialty pathway.

units.title: Development of vision, visual behavior and pediatric assessment
objectives: Describe maturation of visual function and age-appropriate methods for measuring acuity and fixation.
Structure a pediatric eye assessment using history, monocular visual function, pupils, alignment/motility and anterior/posterior segments.
Distinguish a screening referral from a diagnostic examination.
topics: visual development; fixation preference; age-appropriate acuity; cycloplegic refraction; consent and family communication
task-based observation of pediatric behavior and portable examination technology (recording is illustrative, not a device-accuracy guideline)
boardDomains: Core ophthalmic knowledge; pediatric eye exam
units.assessment: Submit a one-page age-stratified examination flowchart and a 5-minute oral presentation.

units.title: Amblyopia: detection, differential and treatment reasoning
objectives: Identify deprivation, strabismic and refractive mechanisms and mixed presentations.
Explain why refractive correction precedes or accompanies penalization in appropriate cases.
Plan follow-up questions and identify recurrence/adherence issues without giving a specific patient treatment plan.
topics: critical period; fixation/acuity asymmetry; refractive amblyopia; optical correction; occlusion/atropine concepts; adherence
amblyopia mechanisms and evidence-aware treatment categories; not a patient-specific prescription
units.assessment: Write a comparative options matrix with evidence caveats, family burden and follow-up measures.

units.title: Strabismus examination and ocular motor localization
objectives: Interpret cover/uncover and alternate-cover findings; state what each reveals and what it cannot.
Describe alignment at distance and near, versions/ductions, head posture, sensory status and diplopia history.
Generate a differential for acquired deviation including neurologic or orbital red flags.
topics: prism cover testing; comitance; torsion; sensory status; cranial nerve patterns; acute acquired deviation
developmental ocular motor anatomy and the distinction between congenital dysinnervation and acquired localization
casePractice: Infantile esotropia; Duane syndrome; Brown syndrome
units.assessment: Submit a structured motility exam interpretation from a linked case, without copying any image.

units.title: Esotropia and exotropia: classification and evidence-based pathways
objectives: Classify common comitant deviations and differentiate accommodative from partially accommodative patterns.
Use cycloplegic refraction and alignment measurements to form a reasoned differential.
Recognize when apparent deviation or neurologic signs call for a broader workup.
topics: infantile/accommodative esotropia; intermittent exotropia; sensory strabismus; deviations by age and onset
infantile-onset esotropia: phenotype, developmental history, comorbidity, measurement and individualized timing decisions
units.assessment: Case conference: state problem representation, differential, next examination/test, and uncertainty.

units.title: Diplopia, incomitance and adult strabismus
objectives: Characterize binocular diplopia, onset, gaze dependence and torsion.
Differentiate common age-related, restrictive, paralytic, thyroid-associated and postoperative patterns.
Identify urgent features that require neurologic/orbital evaluation rather than routine strabismus pathway.
topics: adult diplopia; cranial nerve palsy; thyroid eye disease; sagging eye syndrome; post-surgical deviation; cyclovertical strabismus
adult-onset diplopia and vertical/torsional patterns; restriction, cranial neuropathy, thyroid-associated and post-ocular-surgery differentials; urgent causes remain clinician-assessed
casePractice: Sagging eye syndrome; strabismus with scleral buckle; acquired Brown syndrome
units.assessment: Create an adult diplopia triage map with explicit red flags and referral boundaries.

units.title: Strabismus treatment principles and surgical reasoning
objectives: Compare optical, amblyopia-directed, prism, observation and surgical strategies at a conceptual level.
Explain how surgical choices depend on measurements, prior surgery, anatomy, goals and surgeon judgement.
Communicate that videos and cases do not authorize or teach independent surgery.
topics: surgery decision factors; reoperation; adjustable sutures; oblique muscle patterns; postoperative diplopia
reoperation, torsion, restrictive mechanics and risk-aware case discussion; videos teach recognition, not surgery
casePractice: Case index and surgical videos (observational only)
units.assessment: Write a non-operative decision memo explaining indication questions and alternatives, not a surgical plan.

units.title: Pediatric cataract, glaucoma and anterior segment disease
objectives: Recognize why congenital/infantile cataract and glaucoma can threaten visual development.
Build a differential for leukocoria and identify urgent referral concerns.
Explain that timing and surgery decisions are individualized and depend on specialized teams.
topics: congenital cataract; glaucoma; anterior segment dysgenesis; leukocoria; visual axis; aphakic correction concepts
pediatric uveitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis association, infectious/mimic differential and the need to check current screening and treatment guidance
units.assessment: Prepare a leukocoria differential and escalation memo with sources and no diagnosis from a photograph alone.

units.title: Retinopathy of prematurity and pediatric retina
objectives: Summarize ROP pathophysiology and the purpose/limits of screening.
Explain why screening timing and follow-up depend on birth history and evolving findings and must follow current local protocol.
Recognize need for urgent specialist coordination and the consequences of missed follow-up.
topics: ROP screening; zone/stage/plus concepts; treatment options at overview level; follow-up continuity; pediatric retinal dystrophy overview
ROP follow-up is a continuity/safety problem; recordings found here do not supply a full current screening/treatment curriculum
units.assessment: Design a process-safety checklist for tracking screening and follow-up; no patient-specific schedule.

units.title: Nystagmus, neuro-ophthalmology and developmental visual disorders
objectives: Characterize nystagmus onset, waveform/context and associated visual/systemic findings.
Identify optic nerve, neurologic, sensory and developmental causes requiring coordinated evaluation.
Explain why examination and targeted testing, not one isolated sign, support localization.
topics: infantile nystagmus; optic nerve hypoplasia; cortical/cerebral visual impairment; ocular motor apraxia; neurologic red flags
cerebral/cortical visual impairment, ocular motor developmental patterns and multidisciplinary communication
casePractice: Optic nerve hypoplasia; septo-optic dysplasia; Moebius syndrome; nystagmus
units.assessment: Use a linked case to draw a differential tree and specify what evidence would change it.

units.title: Genetics, systemic associations, imaging and tests
objectives: Construct a focused ocular/systemic history for inherited or developmental disease.
Interpret the role and limits of OCT, ERG, ocular imaging and genetic testing at a high level.
Use multidisciplinary referral and avoid interpreting an isolated test as a diagnosis.
topics: ocular genetics; syndromic anterior segment; retinal dystrophy; ERG; OCT; consent and genetic counselling boundaries
clinical imaging/devices, genetic contributions and limits of observational or research evidence
casePractice: Blue cone monochromacy; FEVR; Marfan/related disorders case-index leads
units.assessment: Submit a test-selection rationale for a fictional scenario, listing limitations and collaborators.

units.title: Urgent presentations, ocular trauma, infection and safeguarding
objectives: Recognize red eye, orbital cellulitis, trauma, leukocoria and acute visual change as potentially urgent.
Form a differential while separating time-critical action from diagnostic certainty.
Document concerns objectively and use local safeguarding/reporting pathways; avoid unsupported attribution.
topics: orbital cellulitis; endophthalmitis; trauma; non-accidental injury differential; acute vision loss; consent
urgent leukocoria/abnormal red-reflex differential, inflammatory red flags and escalation rather than image-only diagnosis
casePractice: Orbital cellulitis; trauma; retinal hemorrhage differential; retinoblastoma
units.assessment: Write a brief simulated escalation note with red flags and uncertainty; no real-patient details.

units.title: Quality improvement, research literacy and lifelong learning
objectives: Critically appraise a guideline or study for population, outcome, limitations and currency.
Design a small follow-up or screening quality-improvement question without asserting case volumes.
Explain how practice guidelines inform but do not replace clinician judgement.
topics: study design; guideline currency; research ethics; follow-up; access and equity; audit; communicating uncertainty
reading presentation and limits of pediatric ophthalmology research, registry and practice-improvement evidence
casePractice: No patient images required; use cited public guidelines and synthetic vignettes clearly labelled fictional
units.assessment: Submit a 1,000-word evidence brief using a 4-level rubric below.

assignment.title: Integrated portfolio: pediatric eye and alignment reasoning
deliverables: Two linked-source case analyses, one pediatric and one adult, each with problem representation, differential, evidence needed, red flags, family communication, and uncertainty. Use links only; do not copy identifiable images, patient records or screenshots.
A 1,000-word evidence brief on a current pediatric ophthalmology topic with a source-date check and a short bias/limitations appraisal.
A process map for screening/referral/follow-up coordination (not an individual infant schedule or treatment order).
Complete the 10 original questions and explain why each distractor is inferior.

rubric.fullCredit: Separates findings from inference; offers reasonable alternatives and red flags; does not overstate certainty.
Uses authoritative source directly; identifies date, population and limits; checks changing policy.
Includes age-appropriate assessment, family-centred explanation, and appropriate referral/escalation boundaries.
Uses source links with attribution; no copying patient images or records; fictional scenarios labelled.

assignment.scoring: Each criterion receives 0=missing/unsafe, 1=partial, 2=competent for self-study, 3=strong; weighted total mapped to 0–100 for feedback only. No validated board-passing predictor, clinical sign-off or credential.

assessment.formative: Each unit: retrieval quiz, linked-case reasoning, short written reflection and objective checklist; every case answer must identify an uncertainty and safety boundary.
assessment.summative: 10 original multiple-choice items with rationales plus portfolio scored using rubric; self-study feedback only.
assessment.passingStandard: No validated passing threshold. Suggested self-study goal ≥80% after remediation is a learner-selected mastery target, not an exam prediction or guarantee.
assessment.boardMappingNotice: Domains are an educational crosswalk to broad ophthalmic knowledge/reasoning, not an official ABO subspecialty blueprint. No proprietary board material used.

studyHours.plan: 120 self-study hours over 12 weeks (10 h/week): 36 h planned future lecture production (not presently delivered), 36 h readings/case review, 24 h question retrieval/reflection, 24 h portfolio/revision. These are study-plan allocations only, not verified media time or clinical training.

mapping.name: Pediatric Ophthalmology and Adult Strabismus Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Johns Hopkins describes a 12-month clinical fellowship with clinics/surgery, academic sessions, a year-long didactic curriculum, journal clubs and research. Its page reports a local 2024–25 fellow log (274 supervised primary-surgeon strabismus cases and other subtotals); those are institution-specific historical reported counts, not universal minimums/guarantees. AUPO FCC directory lists the distinct category Pediatric Ophthalmology at Johns Hopkins / The Wilmer Institute, next review 2028. Do not claim ACGME accreditation: the official fellowship page identifies no ACGME status; AUPO FCC compliance is a separate status.

unitMap.text: Development of vision, visual behavior and pediatric assessment
coveredTopics: visual development; fixation preference; age-appropriate acuity; cycloplegic refraction; consent and family communication
task-based observation of pediatric behavior and portable examination technology (recording is illustrative, not a device-accuracy guideline)

unitMap.text: Amblyopia: detection, differential and treatment reasoning
coveredTopics: critical period; fixation/acuity asymmetry; refractive amblyopia; optical correction; occlusion/atropine concepts; adherence
amblyopia mechanisms and evidence-aware treatment categories; not a patient-specific prescription

unitMap.text: Strabismus examination and ocular motor localization
coveredTopics: prism cover testing; comitance; torsion; sensory status; cranial nerve patterns; acute acquired deviation
developmental ocular motor anatomy and the distinction between congenital dysinnervation and acquired localization

unitMap.text: Esotropia and exotropia: classification and evidence-based pathways
coveredTopics: infantile/accommodative esotropia; intermittent exotropia; sensory strabismus; deviations by age and onset
infantile-onset esotropia: phenotype, developmental history, comorbidity, measurement and individualized timing decisions

unitMap.text: Diplopia, incomitance and adult strabismus
coveredTopics: adult diplopia; cranial nerve palsy; thyroid eye disease; sagging eye syndrome; post-surgical deviation; cyclovertical strabismus
adult-onset diplopia and vertical/torsional patterns; restriction, cranial neuropathy, thyroid-associated and post-ocular-surgery differentials; urgent causes remain clinician-assessed

unitMap.text: Strabismus treatment principles and surgical reasoning
coveredTopics: surgery decision factors; reoperation; adjustable sutures; oblique muscle patterns; postoperative diplopia
reoperation, torsion, restrictive mechanics and risk-aware case discussion; videos teach recognition, not surgery

unitMap.text: Pediatric cataract, glaucoma and anterior segment disease
coveredTopics: congenital cataract; glaucoma; anterior segment dysgenesis; leukocoria; visual axis; aphakic correction concepts
pediatric uveitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis association, infectious/mimic differential and the need to check current screening and treatment guidance

unitMap.text: Retinopathy of prematurity and pediatric retina
coveredTopics: ROP screening; zone/stage/plus concepts; treatment options at overview level; follow-up continuity; pediatric retinal dystrophy overview
ROP follow-up is a continuity/safety problem; recordings found here do not supply a full current screening/treatment curriculum

unitMap.text: Nystagmus, neuro-ophthalmology and developmental visual disorders
coveredTopics: infantile nystagmus; optic nerve hypoplasia; cortical/cerebral visual impairment; ocular motor apraxia; neurologic red flags
cerebral/cortical visual impairment, ocular motor developmental patterns and multidisciplinary communication

unitMap.text: Genetics, systemic associations, imaging and tests
coveredTopics: ocular genetics; syndromic anterior segment; retinal dystrophy; ERG; OCT; consent and genetic counselling boundaries
clinical imaging/devices, genetic contributions and limits of observational or research evidence

unitMap.text: Urgent presentations, ocular trauma, infection and safeguarding
coveredTopics: orbital cellulitis; endophthalmitis; trauma; non-accidental injury differential; acute vision loss; consent
urgent leukocoria/abnormal red-reflex differential, inflammatory red flags and escalation rather than image-only diagnosis

unitMap.text: Quality improvement, research literacy and lifelong learning
coveredTopics: study design; guideline currency; research ethics; follow-up; access and equity; audit; communicating uncertainty
reading presentation and limits of pediatric ophthalmology research, registry and practice-improvement evidence

topicGaps: Verified video corpus is far below the 36-hour specialty floor; source-linked EyeRounds clips total only a small amount and many are brief technique demonstrations, not full lectures.

Need full-length recorded teaching across visual development, pediatric assessment, amblyopia, esotropia/exotropia, adult diplopia, ROP, cataract/glaucoma, nystagmus, genetics, emergencies and evidence appraisal.
Individual JHU/AAO/AAPOS linked video runtimes and/or playback availability remain unverified and contribute zero hours.
No common foundation hours are counted; no duplicates, playlists, planned content, or estimated durations counted.
Only 13.024167 verified free specialty-video hours are presently identified against the 36-hour floor; residual gap is 22.975833 hours. Scripted episodes are not rendered and add zero video hours.

Substantial gaps remain in full, coherent clinician-level courses for pediatric anterior segment disease, cataract/glaucoma, ROP, pediatric retinal dystrophy, genetics/testing, emergency evaluation, and research methods. Several newly found talks are topical webinars rather than comprehensive courses.

AAPOS describes historical meeting recordings as registration-required and paid for non-attendees; they are not freely counted. The 10 appended AAPOS free recordings have observed individual duration evidence and are linked from its complimentary-recording archive.

No foundation hours are counted. Recorded clip time includes topical webinar discussions and is an exposure measure, not equivalent to a formal course, verified learning, training, case volume, or competence.

Official U.S. ABO materials describe general ophthalmology certification; this course does not establish a separate U.S. pediatric/strabismus board, ABO eligibility, FEBOS-SP eligibility, fellowship accreditation or surgical experience.

boardNames: American Board of Ophthalmology (ABO) — general ophthalmology certification
European Board of Ophthalmology / ESA / EPOS — FEBOS Strabismus and Paediatric Ophthalmology subspecialty examination (European pathway; distinct from U.S. ABO)
medical.boardStatus: In the United States, ABO describes general ophthalmology certification based on accredited ophthalmology training and written qualifying plus oral examinations. No separate U.S. ABO pediatric ophthalmology/strabismus board exam was identified. Separately, EBO/ESA/EPOS offers the FEBOS-SP European subspecialty examination; it requires EBO-equivalent/UEMS qualifications, specialist registration, a one-year full-time fellowship to ICO-equivalent standards, and substantial verified surgical experience; those criteria are not met or conferred by this course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent educational curriculum grants no ABO or FEBOS-SP eligibility, accredited training, clinical privileges, licensure, case volume or procedural competence. Consult each board for current rules; no eligibility determination is made.

practiceQuestions.stem: A preschool child has reduced monocular acuity and a substantial interocular refractive difference on a comprehensive exam. What is the best conceptual next step in an amblyopia plan?

options.text: Ignore refraction and operate on extraocular muscles
Address refractive correction and assess/monitor amblyopia in the full clinical context
Diagnose retinal dystrophy from acuity alone
Patch both eyes equally without reassessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: Amblyopia is a developmental visual disorder with refractive and strabismic causes; treatment decisions require comprehensive examination, optical correction and monitoring. This is a general educational principle, not a prescription.

practiceQuestions.stem: During an alternate cover test, the examiner alternately dissociates the eyes and observes refixation movements. What does this chiefly help quantify?

options.text: Manifest deviation only
Total deviation under dissociation, including latent component
Retinal perfusion
Cycloplegic refractive error

practiceQuestions.rationale: Alternate cover testing dissociates fusion to reveal the total deviation; exact measurement requires proper technique and prism neutralization.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 4-year-old has crossing that improves with glasses. Which measurement is central to evaluating whether an accommodative component is present?

options.text: Cycloplegic refraction and alignment with correction
Color vision only
Visual field alone
Intraocular pressure only

practiceQuestions.rationale: Cycloplegic refraction identifies hyperopia that can drive accommodative convergence, while alignment with correction tests response. See the linked EyeRounds teaching case.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child presents with newly acquired esotropia and headache, vomiting, and abduction limitation. Which course is most appropriate conceptually?

options.text: Assume accommodative esotropia and defer review
Urgently evaluate for neurologic/orbital causes through appropriate clinical pathway
Prescribe patching without examination
Use online case images to determine diagnosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: Acute acquired deviation with neurologic symptoms/limitation is a red-flag pattern; this calls for prompt clinician assessment and broader differential, not a definitive diagnosis from this vignette.

practiceQuestions.stem: A premature infant is being followed for possible ROP. Which statement is safest?

options.text: Screening ends when one examination is normal
Timing and follow-up are determined from birth history and serial findings under current local protocol
A single online video substitutes for specialist examinations
Only symptoms determine need for screening

practiceQuestions.rationale: ROP screening and follow-up are protocol-driven because disease evolves and infants may be asymptomatic; confirm current guidance and local pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with binocular diplopia reports torsional image separation that worsens in specific gaze positions. What is a useful next characterization?

options.text: Ignore gaze dependence
Document onset, gaze dependence, torsion, motility/alignment and neurologic/orbital red flags
Diagnose superior oblique palsy from symptom alone
Recommend an operation based on a video

practiceQuestions.rationale: Diplopia evaluation relies on a structured history and examination; torsion and gaze pattern inform, but do not by themselves settle, the differential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn has leukocoria in a photograph. What is the educationally sound interpretation?

options.text: It is pathognomonic for one benign condition
It has a differential including urgent sight- or life-threatening causes and warrants prompt professional assessment
A photograph alone confirms cataract
Wait for routine school screening

practiceQuestions.rationale: Leukocoria is a sign with a broad differential; a photo cannot establish diagnosis. Prompt specialist assessment is appropriate.
practiceQuestions.domain: Pediatric anterior segment and urgent presentations

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes U.S. and European board pathways?

options.text: ABO has a distinct pediatric ophthalmology certifying examination
ABO general ophthalmology certification uses written and oral examinations; EBO/ESA/EPOS separately offer a European strabismus/paediatric subspecialty exam with its own eligibility
Completion of any online course qualifies for FEBOS
A fellowship alone guarantees U.S. board eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO describes a general ophthalmology two-exam pathway; EBO’s FEBOS-SP is a distinct European subspecialty examination with stringent eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: An online teaching site links authentic patient images and states educational-use terms. What is the compliant course practice?

options.text: Download and rehost all images
Link students to source; follow stated license/credit; do not copy or republish images absent explicit permission
Remove attribution and labels
Assume public viewing equals unrestricted commercial reuse

practiceQuestions.rationale: Public access does not equal unrestricted reuse. EyeRounds terms allow certain educational uses under conditions but prohibit creating one’s own image gallery and financial gain without permission.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which conclusion can a learner draw from a short surgical demonstration video?

options.text: That the learner can independently perform the operation
That the technique exists and can be discussed observationally; competence requires supervised training and assessment
That surgical outcomes are guaranteed
That video replaces accredited fellowship

practiceQuestions.rationale: A demonstration is educational exposure, not skill validation, credentialing, supervised procedural experience, or authorization.

title: Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced learners: ophthalmology residents/fellows or physicians with foundational ocular anatomy, refraction, visual acuity, ocular motility and pediatric development knowledge.
Expected competencies: interpret peer-reviewed clinical guidance, identify limits of a remote self-study, use appropriate source attribution and privacy practices.
No clinical patient contact, hands-on skill, case-volume requirement or procedural training is supplied.
objectives: Conduct a structured age-/development-appropriate pediatric eye history and examination conceptually and distinguish screening from comprehensive evaluation.
Reason across pediatric vision development, amblyopia, strabismus, pediatric anterior-segment disease, ROP, leukocoria, nystagmus and neuro-ophthalmic red flags.
Interpret and communicate alignment/sensory measurements, uncertainty, guideline scope and follow-up needs.
Critically read public practice guidelines and recognize dates, recommendation strength and evidence limitations.
Separate clinical fellowship training, AUPO programme approval, AAPOS membership and ABO/ABMS board certification.
Apply privacy, case-image licensing and non-republication requirements.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course is independent education and grants no institutional affiliation, accredited training, licensure, clinical competence, procedure competence, ABMS/ABO eligibility, AAPOS membership or certification. ABO certification is primary ophthalmology certification and requires its own qualifying training and written/oral examinations. As checked 2026-10-07, the ABMS certificate directory lists Ophthalmology under ABO and “No Subspecialties”; no separate ABMS/ABO pediatric ophthalmology/strabismus board exam or certificate was identified. AAPOS membership and AUPO FCC-approved fellowship status are separate association/program designations, not board certification. Verify current board and fellowship rules directly.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 4-year-old is referred after an unreliable vision screen. What is the best next conceptual step?

options.text: Repeat screening indefinitely until a pass
Arrange comprehensive eye evaluation because failed/unreliable testing warrants referral
Diagnose amblyopia from the screen alone
Wait until school age

practiceQuestions.rationale: The Pediatric Eye Evaluations PPP recommends comprehensive evaluation when screening fails or the child cannot be tested reliably; the screen is not a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which sequence is most consistent with the pediatric examination PPP when feasible?

options.text: Cycloplegia, then alignment and sensory testing
Sensory testing before dissociating tests; binocular alignment before cycloplegia
Fundus photography before history
Cover one eye throughout all tests

practiceQuestions.rationale: The PPP advises sensory tests before dissociating maneuvers and binocular alignment testing before cycloplegia, while adapting to cooperation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 5-year-old has an intermittent outward deviation and good fusional control. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Every intermittent exotropia requires immediate surgery
Observation may be reasonable in selected young children with good control; assess trend and sensory status
No follow-up is needed
Amblyopia cannot coexist

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO PPP says young children with intermittent exotropia and good control may be followed; worsening control/stereoacuity can affect treatment consideration.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which measurement assesses manifest strabismus?

options.text: Prism and alternate cover test
Simultaneous prism and cover test
Cycloplegic refraction
Hirschberg estimate only

practiceQuestions.rationale: The simultaneous prism-and-cover test measures manifest deviation; prism alternate-cover testing measures total misalignment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child develops new acquired esotropia. Which approach is best?

options.text: Assume benign accommodation without examination
Promptly evaluate for cause and associated neurologic/restrictive features
Wait for spontaneous resolution for a year
Prescribe patching without assessment

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO PPP highlights prompt evaluation and treatment for acquired esotropia; differential and urgency depend on findings.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has an asymmetric white reflex on screening. What is the safest educational inference?

options.text: It is normal variation and needs no follow-up
It is an abnormal red-reflex finding requiring prompt specialist evaluation
It proves retinoblastoma
It proves congenital cataract

practiceQuestions.rationale: Leukocoria/asymmetric reflex has a broad differential but is abnormal and merits prompt evaluation; the finding alone does not establish a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which findings should be documented alongside measured deviation?

options.text: Only the prism number
Test method, target/distance, correction status, motility, sensory function and cooperation
Only caregiver’s impression
Only whether surgery was discussed

practiceQuestions.rationale: Interpretability depends on method, viewing conditions, refractive correction, sensory and motor exam, and the child’s cooperation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about AAPOS is accurate?

options.text: AAPOS membership is a pediatric ophthalmology board certification
AAPOS is a professional association whose member criteria include ophthalmology certification plus additional approved fellowship training
AAPOS administers ABO oral exam
AAPOS membership guarantees competence

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAPOS describes membership requirements, but the association is distinct from ABO/ABMS certification and does not make this self-study a credential.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about EyeRounds clinical images is correct?

options.text: Free viewing means unrestricted rehosting
Images may be copied to a commercial course without permission
Terms allow limited noncommercial educational use with attribution, but prohibit building a photo gallery; link rather than rehost
Images should be stripped of credits

practiceQuestions.rationale: EyeRounds terms state limited noncommercial educational use, attribution and restrictions on reuse and financial gain; source case/image links are retained.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the status of this course in relation to ABO certification?

options.text: Completion awards pediatric ophthalmology board certification
It replaces accredited ophthalmology residency
It is independent self-study; ABO certification has its own accredited-training eligibility and written/oral examinations
It grants surgical privileges

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABO describes primary ophthalmology certification examinations and training; this independent course cannot confer eligibility, certification, or privileges.
